Title: Meta’s TikTok Ad Ban Turns Platform Rivalry Into a Traffic War

URL Source: https://wersm.com/meta-tiktok-ad-ban-platform-rivalry-traffic-fight/

Published Time: 2026-10-13T11:46:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
Meta has drawn a sharper line between competing platforms. Since October 8, it has reportedly stopped accepting advertising from TikTok parent ByteDance across Facebook and Instagram in seven markets: the United States, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam.

The more consequential part is that the restriction reportedly reaches beyond ByteDance’s own media buying. Third-party advertisers running campaigns that send people to TikTok or other ByteDance properties may also be affected. That turns a rivalry between two social platforms into a dispute over who gets to control the route between paid media and audience attention.

## Meta is blocking the destination, not just the competitor

The change was first reported by [Bloomberg](https://bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/meta-bans-tiktok-parent-bytedance-from-advertising-on-its-apps-in-7-countries) and summarized in detail by [Adweek](https://www.adweek.com/social-marketing/meta-tiktok-ad-ban-advertisers/). According to the reports, Meta began enforcing the restriction on Thursday, October 8, and applied it to ads and paid marketing messages from ByteDance.

Meta’s stated logic is direct. Spokesperson Chris Sgro said the company does not have to provide promotional services to a competitor whose goal is to pull people away from its apps. Meta framed the decision as ordinary competitive behavior rather than an exceptional platform policy.

But the reported inclusion of third-party campaigns changes the practical meaning. A brand may not be advertising TikTok itself, yet still use a Facebook or Instagram campaign to send viewers to a TikTok creator, product page or account. If those destinations are rejected, Meta is no longer simply deciding which advertisers it wants to serve. It is deciding which external destinations its paid distribution can support.

## The creator campaign problem is bigger than the TikTok ban

This matters because creator campaigns are rarely confined to one platform. A brand may discover a creator on TikTok, build a campaign around that creator’s style, and then use Meta’s targeting and reach to extend the campaign to another audience. The media plan depends on the platforms behaving like connected channels, even when the companies themselves are direct competitors.

Meta’s move breaks that assumption. Advertisers may have to separate creative, landing pages and measurement more aggressively by platform. A campaign that once used Instagram or Facebook to drive attention toward TikTok may need a Meta-native destination, a neutral website, or a different creator activation entirely.

That is an immediate operational headache, but the larger signal is strategic. The major platforms are becoming less willing to function as neutral distribution layers for one another. They still compete for advertisers, creators and attention, but now they are also competing over the exits from their own environments.

For marketers, the lesson is not simply to move budget away from Meta or TikTok. It is to stop treating platform access as interchangeable. A campaign built around one platform’s creator graph, links and measurement tools can become fragile when a rival changes the rules overnight.

The next phase of social advertising may therefore be defined by destination control. Platforms will keep selling reach, but they will increasingly decide which kinds of attention, traffic and commercial intent are allowed to leave.

# Your Algorithm,Your Words:New Ways to Shape What You See on Facebook

October 13, 2026 October 13, 2026

Listen to Article 10 Pause 10

[Audio 2](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/elevenlabs-50620-1791907556.mp3)

![Image 6: Your algorithm logo](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Your-Algorithm_Your-Words_New-Ways-to-Shape-What-You-See-on-Facebook_Header.jpg)

![Image 7](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/plugins/post-media-zip/assets/downloadicon_arrow.png)Download image

## Takeaways

*   We’re introducing new AI-powered tools that help you shape what you see in Feed and Reels by telling us what you’re interested in,in your own words.
*   With Your algorithm and new feedback options,you can directly input your interests to fine-tune what you see,and our ranking systems will adapt in real-time.
*   We’ve also updated the three-dot menu to make it easier to access these customization tools.

Facebook is at its best when it helps you find and do more of what you’re actually into.Now we’re putting you in the driver’s seat.New AI-powered tools let you tell Facebook,in your own words,what you want to see in Feed and Reels,and your recommendations respond right away.  
  
You can now fine-tune your experience and interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what you see on Facebook,meaning you’ll see recommendations that are more relevant,more nuanced,and more you.We’ve updated the three-dot menu on every post to make it easier to access these new customization tools.

## Talk to Your Algorithm,Fine-Tune What You See

We’re rolling out Your algorithm,where you can directly add and manage the topics you want to see in Feed and Reels.Think of it as a dedicated space to tell us exactly what you’re into.You can find it in the three-dot menu.

[Video 5](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/01_Your-Algo_01.mp4)![Image 8](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/plugins/post-media-zip/assets/downloadicon_arrowimg.png)Download video

[Video 6](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/01_Your-Algo_reels_02.mp4)![Image 9](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/plugins/post-media-zip/assets/downloadicon_arrowimg.png?resize=18%2C18)Download video

## More Ways to Tell Us What You Want,In Your Own Words

See something you love,or something that’s not for you?We’re introducing more ways to provide feedback directly from the posts you see in Feed and Reels.After clicking‘Interested’or‘Not interested,’we may ask follow up questions for more detail on what you liked or disliked.You can easily tell us,in your own words,what you want to see more or less of,and your recommendations will update in real time.It’s a more direct,conversational way to shape your experience.

[Video 7](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/02_More-Ways-to-Tell-Us-What-You-Want-In-Your-Own-Words_Carousel-01.mp4)![Image 10](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/plugins/post-media-zip/assets/downloadicon_arrowimg.png)Download video

[Video 8](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/02_More-Ways-to-Tell-Us-What-You-Want-In-Your-Own-Words_Carousel-02.mp4)![Image 11](https://about.fb.com/wp-content/plugins/post-media-zip/assets/downloadicon_arrowimg.png?resize=18%2C18)Download video

## Smarter,More Interactive Ranking Systems

Our[ranking systems](https://transparency.meta.com/features/ranking-and-content/)work to bring you the content you care about–and they’ve gotten remarkably good at it,inferring what you’re into from what you engage with on Facebook:from the posts you like and comment on to what you watch(among thousands of other signals).Now,large language models are helping us take a genuine leap forward.

LLMs can incorporate the interests,context,and intent behind natural language,unlocking an algorithm you can actually talk to.Tell it what you want more or less of,and your recommendations respond in real time,adapting within the same session to reflect what matters to you right now.

Under the hood,this marks a real evolution in how ranking works:by bringing freeform text together with everything we already understand about what you enjoy,the algorithms behind your Feed and Reels keep getting more relevant and responsive over time.

kept.heading: SHOW AI INFLUENCERS WITH REAL PEOPLE (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI influencers are seen as less trustworthy because they can't actually use the products they promote. Showing them in everyday moments with real people, like grabbing coffee or going for a run, helps close that gap. In a study of 9,500+ posts and 4 experiments, these scenes drove 20.7% more engagement and made people up to 17.5% more likely to choose the product.
kept.article_text:
Title: Show AI influencers with real people

URL Source: https://app.sciencesays.com/p/show-ai-influencers-with-real-people

Published Time: 2026-10-13T10:22:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
**This insight is brought to you by…**[**Modash**](https://www.modash.io/roi26?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=roi26)

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/77f7bd83-719b-4faa-a818-86f162305561/image.png?t=1791798758)](https://www.modash.io/roi26?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=roi26)

Need to up your influencer marketing game? Grab your spot (for $0) at the [Return on Influence Festival](https://www.modash.io/roi26?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=roi26) on October 21!

Learn the strategy, systems, and content of some of the best influencer marketers out there, including the:

*   Head of Influencer at **ŌURA**

*   Director of Creator & Influencer Partnerships at **Adobe**

*   Senior Director Social Strategy at **Ogilvy**

*   Global Head of Creator Marketing at **Edelman**

Less “thought leadership.” More “here’s how we actually do it.” [Join for free](https://www.modash.io/roi26?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=roi26) 👇

**Topic**: Social Media | AI  
**For**: B2C  
**Research date**: August 2026  
**Universities**: University of Southern California, University of Bologna, University of Pennsylvania

#### 📈**Recommendation**

On average, human influencers generate more engagement than AI influencers. To make AI influencers more effective, show them interacting with real people in your posts (e.g. going for a “run together” to promote fitness clothing).

People will engage more and be more likely to choose the product the AI influencer is promoting.

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e969d9ed-7871-4cde-95d4-ea97842bd718/Insight__344.png?t=1791369105)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   An image and text analysis of over 9500 AI influencer posts as well as 4 experiments found that:

    *   Only 15% of AI influencer posts show them interacting with someone else

    *   Posts with AI influencers having a social interaction receive 20.7% more engagement and on average 290 more likes or comments

    *   People are up to 17.5% more likely to choose a product promoted by an AI influencer when the post includes them engaging with a real human being

*   The effect:

    *   Strengthens for less human-looking AI influencers (e.g. a Japanese anime-style character)

    *   Disappears when:

        *   There isn’t a social interaction (e.g. a person just standing next to the AI influencer)

        *   When the social interaction is with another AI character

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   We know AI influencers can’t actually experience products in real life. So we see them as less [trustworthy and authentic](https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242921996646?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people).

*   When we see them doing things that humans do, it humanizes them, increasing our trust in them and making the post more impactful.

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   It’s unclear if adding human-like features (e.g. them speaking or making live videos or showing emotions) to an AI influencer might also lead to a similar effect.

*   There may be some situations (e.g. selling fantasy videogames) where an AI influencer being artificial may be helpful. In these contexts, people might prefer when influencers seem less realistic.

#### 👀**Real-life example**

Korean AI influencer rozy.gram has over 160K followers on Instagram.

❌**Issue:**Her posts are mostly solo pictures without her interacting with anyone.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/452778ee-e4f2-4c37-aac6-f4f52f4b0ce9/344_Example.jpeg?t=1791369630)

✅**Solution:**Rozy.gram can make her page more effective by:

*   Showing her interacting with other people (e.g. making a coffee for someone at a coffee shop or walking down the supermarket aisle with someone).

*   Adding [text overlays to her posts](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/the-text-overlay-formula-to-optimize-ads) highlighting what she’s doing.

*   Promoting [innovative or tech-related products](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/virtual-influencers), as AI influencers make people more interested in buying these products than humans.

#### 📖**Research**

_Remember: This is_ _a new_ _scientific discovery. In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people)_). It may also not be generalizable to your situation. If it’s a risky change, always test it on a small scale before rolling it out widely._

#### 🔬**Some of our other work**

_Cool stuff we’ve been working on…_

![Image 4](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/1a2385ef-59e0-4743-bee0-bdfbacfd6361/image.png?t=1791469443)

Squarespace invited me to explain the latest science on how to effectively use social proof on your website.

▶️ **The key takeaway for you**: Don't try to look flawless, focus on being a trustworthy, great choice for your target audience - not everyone.

And, courtesy of Squarespace, you can grab the whole _Science-based Playbook for Effective Social Proof_**at no cost**[here](https://pros.squarespace.com/science-says-playbook?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people).

Here is how else Science Says can help you:

*   📈**Join the**[Science Says Platform](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people)to unlock all 300+ insights and exclusive playbooks

*   📘**Boost your results** with [Science-based Playbooks](https://products.sciencesays.com/?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people) (for Pricing, Ad Creatives, Ecommerce, or SaaS)

*   🔬**Get science-based content for your brand**. Publish [groundbreaking insights](https://www.sciencesays.com/enterprise-services?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-ai-influencers-with-real-people) about AI, marketing, or management that your customers will love.

kept.heading: CAN I GET 3,000 SUBSCRIBERS IN 90 DAYS? (WEBSITE)
kept.blurb: Growth in Public is an experiment by Chenell Basilio to gain 3K email subscribers from social media in 90 days. The site tracks subscriber growth by platform in a live scoreboard and documents which tactics drive signups. After posting just 43 times in the past year and seeing newsletter growth stall, Chenell plans to post daily across LinkedIn and other social platforms to test whether social can become a reliable growth channel again.
kept.article_text:
Title: Growth in Public

URL Source: https://growthinpublic.com/

Markdown Content:
## Previous 90-day benchmark

“3,000 is going to be easy for someone like you, isn't it?”

For context, I have not posted much on social in the last 12 months. Looking at LinkedIn alone, I posted 43 times over the year. And over the last 90 days, I've only posted 8 times (like once every 11 days). This is far from a well-oiled machine 🙂

**8**posts on social in the last 3 months

**313**subs from social in the 90 days before

## The leaderboard

Which platform sends the most people to my newsletter.

1.   1 Substack 19 76% of the total · 1 from tagged links · 0 from shares · 18 synced from Substack · 237 in the 90 days before
2.   2 LinkedIn 4 16% of the total · 2 from tagged links · 2 from shares · 62 in the 90 days before
3.   3 Bluesky 1 4% of the total · 0 from tagged links · 1 from shares · 0 in the 90 days before
4.   4 X / Twitter 1 4% of the total · 0 from tagged links · 1 from shares · 5 in the 90 days before
5.   5 Facebook 0 No signups yet · 0 in the 90 days before
6.   6 Instagram 0 No signups yet · 8 in the 90 days before
7.   7 Threads 0 No signups yet · 1 in the 90 days before

## Follower growth

Followers on each platform, next to the subscribers each one has sent.

[Substack](https://substack.com/@chenell)
**43,200**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**19** subscribers sent so far

[X / Twitter](https://x.com/chenellco)
**18,328**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**1** subscriber sent so far

[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chenellco/)
**14,932**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**4** subscribers sent so far

[Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/chenellco/)
**3,002**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**0** subscribers sent so far

[Threads](https://www.threads.com/@chenellco)
**772**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**0** subscribers sent so far

[Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/growthinreverse.com)
**628**followers

-1 since Oct 12

**1** subscriber sent so far

[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=61576759474808)
**2**followers

Starting count (Oct 12)

**0** subscribers sent so far

## Day by day

New subscribers from social each day. Hover a day to see where they came from.

See the numbers as a table

| Day | Substack | LinkedIn | Bluesky | X / Twitter | Facebook | Instagram | Threads | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 12 | 7 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 10 |
| Oct 13 | 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 5 |
| Oct 14 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Oct 15 | 8 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 9 |

## How I count

Only new email subscribers who came from social media make the board.

### Tagged links

Every link I post carries a tag (like utm_source=linkedin). If someone signs up through it, that platform gets the point.

### Shares

When someone shares my site on a platform, my site notices where the visitor came from and tags the signup for them.

### Nothing else

Newsletter recommendations, search, direct visits and signups I can't trace don't count. Signups on this page only count if you came from social media. Once someone joins, they stay counted, even if they unsubscribe later.

Another **83** new subscribers joined from somewhere else (or I couldn't trace them), so they're not on the board.

## Why I'm doing this

**93% of the creators I've studied have used social media to grow their email lists.** And I did too.

In the early days of Growth In Reverse, I was posting constantly, mostly on old Twitter (RIP). The newsletter grew to 21,000 subscribers in 10 months, and social media played a huge role in that.

Then I "got busy" and stopped posting. In the last 12 months, I've posted just 43 times. That's about 3.5 a month, and most of those were me checking the "I posted today" box.

My newsletter growth reflects that. It's been flat for a while, and I want to change that.

**So for 90 days, I'm trying to get 3,000 new email subscribers from social media.** Only social. No recommendations, no referrals, no other sources. I'm only counting people who came through social media.

### 3 questions I want to answer

1.   What's working on social right now to drive subscribers?
2.   Can I turn social back into a reliable growth channel?
3.   Do I want to be back on social media long term?

### The plan

I'm still figuring it out. What I do know: I'll create mostly for LinkedIn and repost to Substack, X, Threads and Facebook. The goal is to post daily (maybe more if it's working).

### Will I hit it?

Honestly, probably not. I haven't posted consistently in a while, so this feels a little like starting over. That's why it's an experiment.

Chenell

**93%**of creators I've studied grew with social

**21,000**subscribers in my first 10 months

**43**posts in the last 12 months

## Want the full breakdown?

What's working, what's not, and the numbers behind it.

kept.heading: SHOPPING IS PART OF THE PRODUCT (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI is changing e-commerce discovery by presenting shoppers with product shortlists instead of sending them to search results. A study on AI Mode found that 74% of participants chose the top-ranked product, while only 10% chose a product ranked third or lower. The author outlines a five-stage organic growth loop: earn AI recommendations through product feeds and third-party signals, convert visitors with tools such as quizzes, encourage user-generated content through packaging and product experiences, generate repeat purchases through customer relationships, and build brand recall. Shopping infrastructure and marketing automation are increasingly table stakes, while customer relationships, creator partnerships, community, first-party data, and brand recall create longer-term advantages.
kept.article_text:
Title: Shopping is part of the product

URL Source: https://www.growth-memo.com/p/organic-growth-in-e-commerce-in-2027

Published Time: 2026-10-12T14:29:07+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qgVk!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4000dd54-7c3b-4c66-a98d-338ca0d1d9c4_1672x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qgVk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4000dd54-7c3b-4c66-a98d-338ca0d1d9c4_1672x941.png)

This Memo was sent to 29,703 subscribers. Welcome to +164 new readers! Sign up for free to get new insights every week, or sign up for Premium to get exclusive tools and frameworks that make you more effective.

I’m in London, speaking at Semrush Spotlight this week. Come, say hi! Quick shoutout to our friends at [dofollow.com](https://trydofollow.io/Growth-Memo), whose Visibility+ service helps B2B SaaS brands uncover where they’re missing from AI answers and traditional search—and close those visibility gaps. If you want to see where competitors may be showing up before you,[see where your brand is missing →](https://trydofollow.io/Growth-Memo)

39% of US consumers have used AI for shopping, according to [Adobe](https://business.adobe.com/blog/ai-traffic-surge-retail-sites-not-machine-readable), and [Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com/news/press-releases/2025/12/05/cyber-week-ai-agents-sales/) says AI influenced 20% of purchases during last year’s BFCM. But only [11% let AI make purchases for them](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-27-gartner-survey-finds-consumers-want-ai-shopping-help-but-not-ai-purchase-decisions).

So AI’s influence sits in product recommendations, aka the shortlist. And the shortlist gets built from what your customers do after they buy: the reviews they write, the videos they post, the brand names they search. Here is how to build a compounding loop around that new behavior.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bCg-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39002438-b0e2-4858-89d3-6120bbad8ada_2048x1152.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bCg-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39002438-b0e2-4858-89d3-6120bbad8ada_2048x1152.png)

Growth Memo research has repeatedly shown that users accept and trust the shortlist AI serves them: [88% of participants in our AI Mode](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/how-consumers-navigate-high-stakes) user behavior study took the shortlist as-is. Consequently, 64% of users clicked nothing on average, and only 23% visited an external site (directly, without clicking a link). Another user behavior study about shopping in ChatGPT shows [93% of sessions had no meaningful click-out](https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/the-shortlist-is-the-new-shelf); only 3% verified the answer on the open web.

AI Visibility strongly impacts the products users pick: In ChatGPT, **AI share of voice and user choice correlate at [0.57 on average](https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/the-shortlist-is-the-new-shelf)**. The range runs from grocery (1.0) and supplements (0.9) down to fitness apps (-0.4) and coaching (-1.0). Being at the top of the shortlist is vital: 74% of participants in our study picked the top ranked product in AI Mode. Rank 3 and below get 10%.

The only exception: Shoppers pick a brand they recognize over rank 1. In our AI Mode study, shoppers named brand recognition as a trust signal in [34% of sessions, vs. 23% in classic search](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/how-consumers-navigate-high-stakes). IAB Australia found [59% of AI shoppers trust AI more](https://business.pureprofile.com/australia-new-zealand-commerce-discovery-report-2026/) when they’ve seen the brand advertised elsewhere.

That differs strongly from Search, where [56% of participants built their own shortlist](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/how-consumers-navigate-high-stakes) (compared to 5% in AI Mode) and only 21% adopted the shortlist shown in AI Overviews. So, the more Google funnels users into AI Mode, the more important it is to appear in product shortlists.

[![Image 3: Shortlist behavior in AI Mode vs. classic search](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vten!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2eef2ad1-6227-4454-859c-9348a952e9a3_2046x1151.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vten!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2eef2ad1-6227-4454-859c-9348a952e9a3_2046x1151.png)

Keep in mind Search is about product grids: [96% of shopping queries surface product grids](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/organic-rankings-vs-product-grids) in an analysis of 4K commercial queries. Shopping Search is not about blue links anymore. When AIOs appear, they [cut clicks on blue links in half](https://www.advancedwebranking.com/free-seo-tools/google-organic-ctr).

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!30Ws!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff63e5ebb-efbe-445c-9817-a9aa7764190c_2048x1152.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!30Ws!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff63e5ebb-efbe-445c-9817-a9aa7764190c_2048x1152.png)

For AI shortlists, tactics you can control (like optimizing your product feed and onsite optimization) only get you so far. AI leans heavily on 3rd-party signals like video, web mentions, and reviews. AI visibility in Google’s AI Overviews has much stronger correlations with YouTube mentions 0.7, branded web mentions 0.7, branded anchors 0.6 and branded search volume 0.4 than metrics like DR 0.3 or referring domains 0.3, according to an [ahrefs study](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-brand-visibility-correlations/). This citation pattern is confirmed in another analysis by [Peec AI](https://peec.ai/blog/top-domains-cited-by-ai-search-analysis-based-on-30m-sources): Youtube is repeatedly cited as one of the strongest citation sources in AI Mode, AI Overviews, Gemini, and Perplexity.

The catch: none of these signals show up in a last-click report. A creator video that puts you on ChatGPT’s shortlist gets no credit when the shopper buys later. That’s why this episode’s sponsor, AirOps, runs a live session on investing in AI search before measurement catches up!

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HEjE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb714310-cfb8-4312-9968-2466caefa982_1080x1080.png)](https://www.airops.com/events/webinar-ai-search-measurement-bain-airops?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=NA_en_Webinar_Perfect-AI-search-measurement_Q4-2026)

Join Matt Hammel, COO of AirOps, and Zak Prauer, Expert Partner, Marketing at Bain & Company, on **Wednesday, October 15, at 3pm ET / 12pm PT**. You’ll learn why every major channel mattered before anyone could measure it, why being recommended matters more than being cited, and how to keep pushing for better evidence without underinvesting.

[Save your spot](https://www.airops.com/events/webinar-ai-search-measurement-bain-airops?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=NA_en_Webinar_Perfect-AI-search-measurement_Q4-2026)

I divide organic growth for ecommerce into 5 steps:

1.   Being visible in the AI shortlist

2.   Capturing more value out of the traffic we still get

3.   Optimizing packaging for engagement

4.   Investing in ongoing relationships

5.   Driving brand trust and recall

At first glance, that’s a funnel with a few extra steps. But each stage hands its output to the next one. The shortlist earns the visit, the visit sells the product, first use builds the relationship, the relationship builds recall, and recall puts you back on the shortlist.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oKD4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff0785bd1-e1af-4f7a-a75f-435c90416070_2900x3420.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oKD4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff0785bd1-e1af-4f7a-a75f-435c90416070_2900x3420.png)

The ecommerce ecosystem around Google, OpenAI, Shopify, and others is building the infrastructure of the future: shopping protocols. Product feeds mattered to earn appearances in Google’s product grids. Now, they’re critical for AI visibility and direct checkout.

Shopping protocols answer 3 questions for an agent:

1.   What’s available?

2.   Can I buy it?

3.   What happened to the order?

Shopify found a [2x higher conversion rate](https://www.shopify.com/editions/spring2026) for product listings in its catalog.

**Do:**

1.   Connect feeds and checkout through UCP or ACP. Fill every feed field and use high-quality images.

2.   Collect verified reviews on Trustpilot and your site.

3.   Lead product titles with your differentiator. Descriptions say who it’s for, how it performs, and how it compares.

4.   Answer 8 to 10 real buyer questions on each product and category page.

If you want to know how your product pages hold up before AI builds its next shortlist, the [E-GEO Audit Tool](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/e-geo-audit-tool) in the premium library scores your product descriptions against the features that are proven to lift visibility in AI shopping recommendations. Pair it with the[Agentic Commerce Playbook](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/agentic-commerce-playbook), a 70+ item checklist for getting products into ChatGPT, Copilot, and AI Mode, phase by phase. Both are in the [Growth Memo Premium Resource Library](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/exclusive-growth-premium-resources).

AI sends fewer, more qualified visitors, but they still need confidence on fit, taste, and comparison. Tools like quizzes, calculators and buyer guides help them decide and help you capture valuable 1st party data.

Quizzes [can convert around 5%](https://revenuehunt.com/state-of-product-recommendation-quizzes/) of takers into orders, roughly 2.75x the typical conversion rate. Beauty merchant Lawless built its quiz around the one question ChatGPT can’t settle for a shopper: which concealer shade fits. It [converts at 36%](https://www.tangent.ai/lawless-beauty-case-study), with 80% completion and a 34% higher AOV.

Quizzes also build a first-party email list. Octane AI, which sells quiz software, reports that its quizzes average a[29% email opt-in rate](https://www.octaneai.com/solutions/lead-generation) and capture 3x more emails than static signup forms. In its case study, Jones Road Beauty collected[800K email leads from its quiz](https://octaneai.com/customers/jones-road-beauty-2023), 80% of the brand’s 1M subscribers. Both numbers come from Octane AI’s own marketing, so read them as a best case. Still, there is something to it: a quiz asks for an email at the moment a shopper wants an answer.

Of course, that can also look “agentic”: Klaviyo’s support agent now resolves [up to 65% of questions](https://www.klaviyo.com/solutions/ai/customer-agent), providing real value to shoppers and merchants.

**Do:**

1.   Pull 20 buyer questions from support tickets, reviews, and Reddit.

2.   Turn them into a quiz, calculator, or finder on product pages and the homepage.

3.   Send answers to your email platform as zero-party data and trigger flows from them.

4.   Compare quiz completers’ conversion rate and AOV with sitewide. Target: 2x. Feed repeated bot questions back into product pages.

25B people watched videos with [“unboxing”](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/unboxing-on-youtube/) on Youtube, and we know YouTube mentions correlate strongly with AI mentions (in AI Overviews). Opening the box a product is delivered in is the first real contact with it. With only [3% of users verifying AI answers online](https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/the-shortlist-is-the-new-shelf), this is where perception moves from the AI’s answer to the product.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ryfN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd20f425-ecae-420b-ad58-5530702d7f1c_1536x2048.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ryfN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd20f425-ecae-420b-ad58-5530702d7f1c_1536x2048.jpeg)

Heck, sometimes the box is the product. At Cannes, I saw a $10K Gucci Xbox. Only 100 existed, and they sold out within days.

Packaging signals value: the box sets expectations for quality, price and brand. Ryder’s [study of 1,300 US shoppers](https://www.ryder.com/en-us/insights/white-papers/e-comm/2026-ryder-e-commerce-consumer-study) shows 45% say a great unboxing makes them want to buy again, and 19% say gift-like packaging gets them to post photos or videos. So, packaging _can_ lead to UGC like videos, posts, and reviews that AI uses in answers.

**Do:**

1.   Design the reveal: Make opening and recycling obvious; add one branded moment worth filming.

2.   Ship a 60-second setup video.

3.   Ask for reviews 7 to 14 days after delivery.

4.   Work with YouTube creators on unboxing and product-in-use videos.

5.   Answer real questions in relevant subreddits with a named account that discloses the affiliation.

Before you pitch a creator, it helps to know who AI already listens to in your category. The [Citation Source Mapper](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/citation-source-mapper) finds the domains, people, and formats AI cites for your topic and turns them into a ranked outreach list, so your unboxing collab lands with a channel that already shows up in answers. Then run the [AI Citation Audit](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/ai-citation-audit) on your top product page to see how citation-ready it is. Both are in the [Growth Memo Premium Resource Library](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/exclusive-growth-premium-resources).

As winning new customers through organic search gets harder to attribute, the intuitive reaction is to focus on repeat sales. The math favors the second order. Across 12,000+ [Gorgias](https://www.gorgias.com/blog/repeat-customer-rate) merchants, repeat customers make up 21% of customers and generate 44% of revenue (source). Roughly one in five customers drives nearly half the business, so the first order should start a plan for the second.

Starbucks shows the mechanism at scale: today’s purchase builds toward a future benefit. [Rewards members drive about 60% of Starbucks’ US revenue](https://s203.q4cdn.com/326826266/files/doc_downloads/investor_day/2026/Tressie-Lieberman-global-chief-brand-officer.pdf) and are 5.6x more likely to visit daily (source).

It doesn’t take a points program, though. Quaker Marine, a nautical clothing brand, sent customers a simple check-in after delivery. Three-week [repurchase rose from 9.7% to 11.2%](https://www.returnsignals.com/blog/quaker-marine-case-study), a 16% lift, without a discount.

Think about this: Shipping confirmation emails have the lowest buying intent ([16% CTR](https://www.omnisend.com/blog/email-marketing-benchmarks/)) but get the most attention ([62% open rate](https://www.omnisend.com/blog/email-marketing-benchmarks/)). Are you using them to educate customers or get them excited about the product?

The pattern behind these examples is a loop inside the loop:

1.   Purchase: the order is placed.

2.   Experience: delivery and first use.

3.   Customer signal: usage, a need or a problem.

4.   Timely response: a reorder prompt, service or a reward.

5.   Repeat purchase: the next order.

Triggered emails are 5.3% of sends, 41% of email revenue and earn 18x revenue per recipient vs. campaigns, according to the [Klaviyo 2026 benchmarks](https://www.klaviyo.com/products/email-marketing/benchmarks).

**Do:**

1.   Build welcome, post-purchase, replenishment, and winback flows.

2.   Split those flows by quiz answers. A field you collect and never use adds nothing.

3.   Time reorder prompts to consumption. Half of second purchases happen within 30 days.

4.   Track loyalty redemption, not enrollment. Active members spend 10% more, redeemers 25%.

5.   Report human CSAT separately so the bot’s numbers can’t hide a decline.

A brand name in the prompt changes the question. Ask ChatGPT for the best minimalist wallet, and it recommends GRAMS28. Ask for the best Ridge wallet for you, and the only question left is which Ridge. Brand searches are sure wins in AI Search, just like in regular search back in the day.

> [Ridge CMO](https://www.omgcommerce.com/ecommerce-evolution-podcast/the-integrated-youtube-influencer-strategy-ridge-wallets-used-to-build-an-60-million-ecommerce-business): “Probably 70% of our sales come from direct, organic, or branded search. And people aren’t just typing in Ridge Wallet for fun. Something makes them want to search that.”

Brand recall is the cheat code that bypasses any shortlist. As the child of the 4 previous stages, recall is driven by 3 factors:

1.   Repeated exposure (creators, ads, word of mouth)

2.   Distinctive cues (name, design, message)

3.   Good experiences (product, packaging, service)

The first 4 stages “feed” all 3. Showing up on AI shortlists and product grids repeats your name (stage 1). The quiz and the bot turn the visit into a good experience (stage 2). The box delivers the distinctive cue and the first-use moment (stage 3). Every check-in and triggered message adds another exposure (stage 4).

Recall comes first in the shopper’s journey, but it takes the longest to build, so it sits last in the loop. Those memories also leave a public footprint of videos, reviews and web mentions, which is what the Ahrefs correlations from earlier pick up.

**Do:**

1.   Ask 5 models what you sell, what it costs, and what your return policy is. Fix what’s wrong at the source.

2.   Use one category descriptor on your site and every third-party profile. Audit for drift.

3.   Publish your own comparison pages before a competitor writes them.

4.   Measure unaided recall quarterly: a post-purchase survey for customers, a broader category sample for the market.

Every stage of the loop has a part competitors can buy and a part they have to earn.

Any competitor can match shopping protocols, crawler access, email and SMS triggers, a support bot, a quiz tool. That makes it table stakes.

The defensible part takes time and effort but compounds: reviews, creator relationships, community, first-party data and the recall that makes shoppers type your name into a prompt.

That split is the [budget question for 2027](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/how-to-plan-2027-when-traffic-is). Fund the copyable half until you’re even with competitors, then put the rest into the half that compounds.

kept.blurb: Creativity comes from experimenting and adapting rather than simply generating a finished result. As AI makes content production faster, marketers risk losing the problem-solving and creative judgment that come from hands-on work. kept.article_text:
Title: What Pokemon Pokopia Taught Me About the Future of Marketing

URL Source: https://sparktoro.com/blog/what-pokemon-pokopia-taught-me-about-the-future-of-marketing/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T05:26:57+00:00

Markdown Content:
I have a marketing prediction: “Made entirely by humans” will become a premium signal. As AI tools make it easier than ever to produce more content, the work that exhibits human creativity and originality will become more valuable. I think we’ll start to see people seeking out human-made work, and paying a premium for the things that demonstrate care and good taste. I mean, it’s kind of already happening now — most obviously with stated preferences. Nobody (sane) is saying they _want_ to consume AI-generated movies and TV shows, or books and blogs.

So… I’ve been playing Pokemon Pokopia. If you’re unfamiliar with this video game, a.k.a. you’re not one of the 5 million Dittos building a better future today, the thing to know is that you’re rebuilding the world with Pokemon and for Pokemon. You make habitats, construct buildings, decorate spaces, and encourage Pokemon to interact with the things you’ve made. There’s cute music and even cuter Pokemon. Part of what I love is that I get to be creative without having to master a traditional creative skill. I don’t know how to paint or draw. The only physically artistic thing I can do is write in cursive, but even then, when I write out my own name, it just looks like a giant sperm. Pokopia gives me a set of tools that lets me build something entirely my own in a cohesive, well-defined aesthetic.

Recently, I tried to build a medieval street in an area called Rocky Ridges, but I didn’t have enough room. So I shifted focus and adapted.

I converted a castle-like structure into a fine dining restaurant for Chef Dante.

![Image 1](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261011-01M4Q7CXT4Z3BSAYS1GNMZ4K64-D262B5B8-983A-4E8E-A17C-42F9B34D7636-1024x581.jpeg)

I created a sitting area with a dinosaur fossil exhibit.

![Image 2](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261011-01M4Q7D25HGK9PNZS4PH9Q1FAT-6BC2A808-13E0-4122-B84B-D177C70D4B5E-1024x581.jpeg)

I built rustic market stalls, including a flower cart and tea stand, and added cash registers to guarantee Pokemon interaction. The result was completely different from what I’d originally envisioned.

![Image 3](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261011-01M4Q76J7RNNR34E3HHC7NBSMD-14129685-B7E3-4F50-AE28-C5684CDB334D-1024x576.jpeg)

And I liked it better.

The best part was watching the Pokemon actually use the space. Seeing them sell their wares, playing with their toys, and [napping on chairs](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261011-01M4Q7D6QHVXBG6RS5GFST82J5-3344F1FB-1E74-4E7E-94C7-C865894335CB.jpeg). _Quel plaisir!_(I don’t know why I said that. I can’t even speak French. I guess it just felt right.)

There was no reason for any of this. This was not a job I was hired for. There was no deadline. And the only customers waiting for me to complete it were my little ‘mon, toddling about aimlessly.

I was just playing.

Then I got to thinking about what it taught me about ~~B2B sales~~ the future of marketing. (I wish I could bridge this thought better by way of Marcel Proust’s “Remembrance of Things Past” but I read that in high school which means… I didn’t actually read it, and I don’t remember it. I just remember my teacher Mr. Beckham [no, not David] talking about the importance of play.)

## What happens when we automate the creative process?

AI is making it possible for marketers to produce more work with fewer resources.

You might hate me for saying this, but… I actually find that idea pretty exciting. And in some ways, it’s what I appreciate about Pokopia. The game removes technical barriers that might otherwise prevent me from expressing a vision. But, of course, there’s a difference between making creativity more accessible and outsourcing the creative decisions themselves.

Imagine if Pokopia introduced a feature where I could type a prompt describing my dream village and the game would build it instantly.

I’d probably try it out of sheer curiosity. Though I sure as heck wouldn’t enjoy it nearly as much. The joy I get from this game is imagining something, trying to make it, encountering obstacles, changing my mind, and stumbling upon something better — or at least more interesting — than I’d originally planned.

I wonder how much of that experience we’re losing in marketing these days. Corporate culture already places enormous pressure on us to do more, faster. More content. More campaigns. More channels. More measurable results. AI offers an obvious solution: outsource more of the work to a computer. But if we automate too much of the creative process, we may also eliminate some of the opportunities that help us become better creative thinkers.

## Taste takes practice

Consider two marketers:

One spends years building their campaigns, making mistakes (and scoring wins too), learning what resonates with audiences, and improving their work. The other becomes exceptionally proficient at using AI to generate campaigns and selecting the best outputs.

They both might produce great work and have solid judgment. But I suspect the first marketer would have practiced skills the second hasn’t had to: real-world problem solving, improvising when things go wrong, and discovering opportunities through the act of making stuff. Those are the skills I expect will become more valuable, and those are the skills I’m interested in honing myself.

As AI makes passable creative work easier to produce, distinctiveness will become harder to find. There’s actually [a 2024 study](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adn5290) that points to this. It found that writers assisted by generative AI were able to produce stories that were rated as more creative, but those stories were also more similar to one another. So while AI can be helpful on a case by case basis, there’s the implication that at scale, it also produces a lot less novel content.

## We need room to play

Play gives us something that optimized production workflows don’t: the freedom to experiment without knowing exactly what the outcome should be. The enjoyment of that is exactly what matters. We keep playing because it’s fun. And so we keep trying out new things, exploring other ideas, satiating curiosities.

I know it’s possible to develop creative judgment through disciplined work, too. But… where’s the fun in that? Nobody aspires to being serious. Ever since I was a little girl, I knew I wanted to increase shareholder value— NO, OF COURSE NOT. I wanted to write articles and make comics and share jokes and take pictures and choose color palettes — as a magazine editor. Sure, I became a content marketer instead, but you see the similarities.

And so I have to ask, if we’re so busy increasing shareholder value that we stop making time to experiment, when do we actually get to develop that taste?

Marketing leaders have a responsibility here. If AI makes teams more productive, — and actually, this is probably a post for another day, but spoiler: _it doesn’t and if anything, it just makes us busier,_[says Harvard on pg. 4](https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf) — then we have a choice. We can fill every newly available hour with more work requests, or we can protect some of that time for experimentation and professional/creative development.

And yes, individual marketers can make choices about which parts of their work they want to automate. But knowing what to automate takes discernment, and yup, good taste, too. You could automate a rote this-for-that task, like populating a cell in a spreadsheet from an updated dataset. But you might be sorry for delegating away creative brief intake to an AI agent because you’ll get dumber from reading less about your own team’s business requests. Because the goal in any marketing job isn’t just to market more. It’s to become better at making and marketing things that are worth paying attention to.

## The premium on human creativity

Back to my original thesis, that “made entirely by humans” will become a premium signal. But 100% human-made doesn’t necessarily guarantee a high bar for quality. Rather, the marketers and creators who earn that premium will be the ones who honed the skills and decision-making that can’t simply be predicted one token at a time: mature creative judgment, distinctive taste, and an original perspective.

AI can help us make things. It can also help us experiment, explore possibilities, and get past the blank page faster. But it’s on us to make sure we actually continue exercising the creative muscles ourselves. If we lose the opportunity or the inclination to play, we risk atrophying some of the very skills that will make us valuable in the future.

And with that, I’m going to take a break to tear down the row of shops I built in Palette Town, and start building some prefab houses with manually-built facades. For the Eeveelutions, Pikachu, and Smeargle, of course.

![Image 4](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261011-01M4Q7BFNPQJGJZG4MQ4N3ZXZN-DC03F53A-85AB-40F7-98EB-3A0D94BF452A-1024x576.jpeg)

_I am irrationally proud of this dual facade for Glaceon and Flareon, the ice and fire Eeveelutions_. _Flareon’s patio even has a brick oven and furnace. IYKYK._

By the way, this essay was also inspired by a 2027 predictions video I made with [Semrush](https://www.semrush.com/). I hope you’ll check that out next. I get a little chaotic in the middle (shocking, I know), but I think it’s a fun watch. 🙂

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeZIMsds4aY)

kept.heading: WHAT DOESN'T GET CHEAPER (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI is making websites cheap enough to build for short-term experiments and one-off events that previously weren't worth the cost. However, enterprise websites still require complex integrations. AI can automate production and support decision-making but cannot eliminate the human effort needed to align stakeholders. Generative tools also create collaboration challenges when multiple companies need to edit the same work. As production costs fall, experimentation will expand while complex projects remain expensive because coordination still requires people.
kept.article_text:
Title: What Doesn't Get Cheaper - Christopher Butler

URL Source: https://www.chrbutler.com/what-doesnt-get-cheaper

Published Time: Mon, 12 Oct 2026 19:02:27 GMT

Markdown Content:
A CEO whose company I’ve followed for a while posted a thesis this week, and I’ve been turning it over since. Websites, he argued, are going the way of contact lenses.

I’ll paraphrase his point below, but [read it for yourself](https://lnkd.in/p/ef6rCCMB). I left [a comment](https://lnkd.in/p/eSd9Gdri) right away, and as I thought about it more, my comment became the rest of what is on this page.

The first contact lenses were expensive and durable. You bought a pair, you cleaned them, you kept them in a case, and you expected them to last. The cost obliged a kind of care. Then the materials improved and production got cheap, and the whole relationship inverted. Now you buy a year of them in a box and throw one away at the end of every day.

His claim is that AI does this to websites. Spin one up, use it, discard it, make another. Iterate fast enough that lifespan stops being a concern.

I think he’s partially right, and, right now, it’s the more interesting part — that’s what makes it feel like it’s the whole.

When production costs drop, the obvious effect is that output gets cheaper and faster. The less obvious effect, and the more important one, is that things become possible that were never attempted before. Not because nobody wanted them, but because they could never justify the floor. A landing page for a two-week experiment. A microsite for one event. A version of an idea built just far enough to find out it was wrong. All of that was priced out of existence until very recently. A long tail of short-lived, exploratory things is going to appear where there was nothing before, and some of it will be genuinely good. _Disposable_ describes them to a point, but just because something can be disposed of doesn’t mean it cannot also last. I suspect that the best of the long tail will last, and grow, and make the tail even longer.

## The Head of the Long Tail

But a tail has a head, and I happen to be standing right on it.

My firm is redesigning and replatforming an enterprise website right now. It has tens of thousands of unique URLs. It depends upon dozens of data integrations. It is a part of a cluster of subdomains doing different things. It has international properties that live on separate infrastructure in other countries because regulation requires it. It contains thousands of pages of product and industry compliance information that has been through legal review and will have to go through it again.

Automation will absolutely reduce the cost of the production involved. It already is. What it will not reduce is everything else, and everything else is most of it.

In a project of this complexity, the challenge is decision-making.

AI can help with that, too, of course. It can index all the website’s content, identify problems, recommend solutions, and organize objectives. A person has to steer it that way, and people have to react. The decisions still land on people.

On this project, there are dozens of stakeholders among several organizations spread across six or seven time zones, which means the work of gathering consensus, sequencing decisions, and unifying expectations costs exactly what it has always cost.

That part hasn’t moved at all.

## Rebuilt by Hand

Here is a specific example of where the head — a project like this — eats its own tail.

We needed to present the brand direction to stakeholders. I worked with the principal designer responsible for the identity work to extend what had been created into a systematized visual language. We established that system in the canvas, and then automated the assembly of a brand presentation deck using a brand system skill. The deck came together almost instantly and was updated several times up until the last possible moment very easily.

The presentation went well. We received feedback both on the deck itself — which needed to be updated and circulated — and on the elements of the brand system it presented. And that’s when the choice to generate a deck rather than build one in a collaborative environment became costly.

Generative work issues from a single account. In this case, there are three separate companies collaborating, so even a shared team account wouldn’t have helped. The prompt is just not as collaborative as the canvas.

What we ended up doing was rebuilding every slide by hand in Figma, not because the generated deck was worse, but because it could only be touched by one person at a time.

The canvas is still the thing: A single surface that several people can stand around and work on at once was an enormous innovation compared to passing a file back and forth, and we’ve had it long enough to take for granted its many efficiencies.

## Reality Catches Up to Perception

People who have been living inside these tools for a couple of years feel like the ground has shifted completely. Then they look up and see everyone still at their desks doing jobs that should have evaporated, and it seems inexplicable.

I’ve been as immersed as anyone, and this project has been a useful correction. The explanation is sitting in the room. There are people in it. If this were a team of three, it would already be mostly automated and I’d be arguing the other side. It isn’t a team of three.

So the long tail will expand, and it will expand dramatically. The disposable things will get made, and they’ll be worth making. But there will still be a head to that tail — slow, expensive, collectively negotiated, anything but disposable.

A disposable lens works because one person wears it for one day. What stays expensive is whatever a great many people have to see through at the same time.

Title: Survey: 32% of US adults prefer highlights over full episodes

URL Source: https://www.advanced-television.com/2026/10/13/survey-32-of-us-adults-prefer-highlights-over-full-episodes/

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://atv-adsrv.com/images/1c8ab29211a7502e2fa93bb4fe02268e.gif)](https://atv-adsrv.com/ads/www/delivery/cl.php?bannerid=824&zoneid=17&source=%7Bobfs%3A%7D&sig=3ea0a43368b0c4a3808c2429cecfd857ff1c02c523ca821408d56a5a828c270c&oadest=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.veexinc.com%2F)

As streaming services compete for attention with social feeds one clip at a time, research reveals that a third of Americans (32 per cent) say they would rather watch highlights from a show than every full episode, rising to 43 per cent among Gen Z.

The survey of 2,500 US adults raises a question about how they watch: are audience attention spans shrinking, or are they simply looking for different ways to watch? Four in ten Americans say they would use streaming services more often if they offered short clips from their shows, rising to more than half (53 per cent) of Gen Z.

[![Image 2](https://atv-adsrv.com/images/3922d909127f9c69c56fa3f2832c94cf.jpg)](https://atv-adsrv.com/ads/www/delivery/cl.php?bannerid=742&zoneid=18&source=%7Bobfs%3A%7D&sig=0f68c0f0f7bf0c00fcc3121a41089f9ba0b57a33c833a3035a8e0c3087ab28ff&oadest=https%3A%2F%2Fjoom.ag%2FRDDd)

That appetite is already reflected in reported viewing habits: 37 per cent of Americans say they use their streaming service more often now that it includes vertical video clips, rising to 47 per cent among Millennials.

But a taste for shorter viewing doesn’t necessarily mean less appetite for a good story. More than half (51 per cent) say clips help them discover shows worth paying to watch. For some, the highlights are the attraction, but for others, those few minutes are what persuade them to settle in for the whole series.

How people access that entertainment matters too. Alongside the appetite for shorter viewing, 61 per cent of Americans say they would be more likely to keep a subscription if they could get it for less through a bundle, giving streaming services and mobile providers two opportunities to explore: more ways to watch and more affordable ways to subscribe.

**Short videos without the social feed?**

For families, the appeal of bite-sized entertainment comes with another question: can children enjoy short videos while spending less time on social media?

More than four in ten Americans (44 per cent) see value in short videos from a brand they trust, while 37 per cent say curated clips would help keep their kids off social media. That figure rises to 47 per cent among Millennials.

The findings come as international restrictions on children’s social media access put alternatives to social platforms under scrutiny. Australia has banned under-16s from social media since December 2025, and the UK government has announced plans to follow suit in 2027.

The US findings suggest an audience for an alternative: curated clips from familiar streaming platforms, giving families another way to enjoy short videos. That appeal could also contribute to what people feel they get for their money. Four in ten Americans (40 per cent) say original or exclusive short videos could help justify the price of a streaming subscription.

**A shorter watch, not necessarily a shorter attention span**

An appetite for highlights does not mean audiences have stopped caring about full-length stories. In the same survey, 65 per cent of Americans say new episodes of shows they follow are important in their decision to keep paying for a streaming service.

The findings suggest there is room for both: something entertaining to watch in a spare moment and a series worth settling in for.

Bango, who sponsored the research, said: “It’s tempting to read these findings as evidence that nobody has the patience for a full episode any more. But people still value the shows they follow. The opportunity is to give them different ways to enjoy that entertainment, depending on the time and attention they want to give it as well as new ways to discover new shows without having to fully commit. For families, there’s another question: can children enjoy short videos without being drawn into a social media feed? Curated, age-appropriate clips from familiar shows could offer another option, particularly as restrictions on children’s social media access take effect. Streaming services have stories and characters people already love. Shorter formats could help audiences enjoy more of those catalogues, while getting a subscription through a phone, broadband or banking bundle could make it more affordable to keep. Together, streaming services with bundlers like telcos and banks can give people more ways to enjoy their favourite entertainment at a price that works for them.”

**Connecting discovery with subscription value**

For telcos, short-form entertainment could strengthen the appeal of the streaming services offered through their bundles, giving customers more ways to enjoy the subscriptions they already pay for.

Younger consumers are already using bundles to manage costs: 21 per cent of Gen Z say they have moved from paying for a service separately to getting it through a bundle to save money in the past year.

Consumers also see value in bundling streaming with other services: 23 per cent say a music subscription would make a streaming service more valuable to them, followed by food delivery benefits (20 per cent) and shopping memberships offering free shipping or discounts (19 per cent).

Bringing discovery, viewing and affordable access together offers streaming providers and telcos a way to respond to different viewing preferences while helping customers get more from the services they choose.

Duo TV follows the learning app’s famous owl and its supporting cast of characters.

Duo the owl has twerked on main, flash mobbed a Charli XCX concert, died, sent his ashes to Dua Lipa, and come back to life. His next big act? Starring in his own animated show.

_DuoTV_ is a new animated series that was created entirely by Duolingo’s in-house design studio. The six-episode series stars in-app characters including Duo himself, the deadpan goth teen Lily, her best friend Zari, and a grumpy bear named Falstaff as they navigate working at a mysterious grocery store called DuoMart. The first two episodes, which will be published on Duolingo’s official YouTube channel and Instagram page, [air on October 12](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Jf2eZ7tI3Os), followed by a new daily episode until the finale.

![Image 33](https://images.fastcompany.com/image/upload/f_webp,q_auto,c_fit,w_1024/wp-cms-2/2026/10/i-2-91621113-duolingo-animated-series.png)

[Image: Duolingo]

For Duolingo, the language and educational learning app, the series is part of a broader mission to deepen the relationship between its fans and its characters. Duo and his motley crew first noticeably entered the zeitgeist [during the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.fastcompany.com/90963949/duolingo-duo-owl-gen-z-obsessed), when the brand’s uniquely irreverent humor on social media helped it amass a major following. In the years since, the brand has continuously upped the ante on investing in its characters and design team to keep users coming back for more.

“We tell everyone right from the get-go, we want to be a hundred-year business,” says Mig Reyes, Duolingo’s head of design. The brand believes that kind of longevity will require more than just an Android and iOS app. Specifically, it’s betting that by building out an entire world around its characters through efforts like _DuoTV_—essentially, creating its own entertainment arm—it can set itself up for the next several decades of business growth.

## Duolingo bets big on character lore

Duolingo has long been the envy of [marketers](https://www.fastcompany.com/section/marketing "Marketing") everywhere for its uniquely beloved mascot and characters, which serve as both the basis of the brand’s marketing flywheel and guides to its in-product features.

In 2024, Duolingo’s CEO, Luis von Ahn, [estimated](https://www.acquired.fm/acq2-episodes/why-duolingo-worked-with-luis-von-ahn-ceo) the owl’s value at “hundreds of millions of dollars” and posited that around 15% of new users come to the app via organic social media. Today, Duo’s fanbase includes 5.3 million Instagram followers, 6.94 million YouTube followers, and 18.2 million [TikTok](https://www.fastcompany.com/section/tiktok "TikTok") followers. Its senior director of brand marketing, Katherine Chan, [told _Fast Company_](https://www.fastcompany.com/91225538/duolingo-ambitious-plan-viral-owl-mascot) in late 2024 that the company aimed to make Duo “more famous than Mickey Mouse.”

Characters like Duo, Lily, and Falstaff serve as great external marketing tools, but Duolingo has also used them to help build out new in-product functions. Lily, for example, is the voice of the brand’s recently debuted [AI-powered speaking function Video Call](https://www.fastcompany.com/91271109/duolingo-most-innovative-companies-2025); while others, like Lucy, Bea, and Zari, guide users through interactive mini podcasts on [DuoRadio](https://blog.duolingo.com/duoradio-listening-practice/). Duo himself has helped to drive major in-app engagement through activations including, in one instance, an update that replaced his normally chipper app icon with a “[dead Duo](https://www.fastcompany.com/91313082/duolingo-dead-duo-owl-social-media-campaign)” (he eventually came back to life).
