kept.article_text:
Title: 38 things we've learned about building AI products

URL Source: https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/38-things-weve-learned-about-building

Published Time: 2026-10-12T18:01:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
We’ve built 10 different AI products at PostHog, including [PostHog AI](https://posthog.com/ai?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), our [install Wizard](https://posthog.com/docs/ai-engineering/ai-wizard?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), [Replay Vision](https://posthog.com/replay-vision?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), [Scouts](https://posthog.com/blog/what-is-a-scout?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), and more. They’re used by nearly 100,000 people every month. This is what we’ve learned.

1.   **[AI can make your product worse](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-features?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#choosing-what-to-build).** It can be slow and unreliable, or solve a problem nobody has (like chatting with your docs, any AI can do this). Just because it’s AI does not mean it’s worth building.

2.   Consider whether you need to build AI at all. It’s often better to[build](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-should-you-build-an-mcp-server-instead)_[for](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm\_source=posthog-newsletter&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-should-you-build-an-mcp-server-instead)_[AI first, like an MCP server](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-should-you-build-an-mcp-server-instead). These are easier to build and maintain. 5x more people use our MCP server daily than PostHog AI.

3.   Look for jobs to be done, not demos. The best opportunities for AI are tasks that take 30+ seconds, use language or interfaces users don’t know (like SQL), or tasks users repeat 20+ times.

4.   Onboarding is a great first target. Our AI install wizard does two hours of work in ~8 minutes. Those who use it[convert to paid 5x more often and activate 2x faster](https://posthog.com/newsletter/context-engineering?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#lesson-6-investing-in-context-pays-off).

5.   Don’t ask “how do we add AI to this?” ask “what is the agent-first version of this?” Doing this forces you to rethink the jobs to be done for an agent-first future and helps you avoid [being disrupted](https://posthog.com/newsletter/2030-shaped-software?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#building-2030-shaped-software-now) by an AI-native competitor.

6.   Building [2030-shaped products](https://posthog.com/newsletter/2030-shaped-software?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#building-2030-shaped-software-now) may require you to start fresh and break from years of cumulative UI and assumptions that are no longer valid or relevant.

7.   Watch for customers[rebuilding your product with AI](https://posthog.com/newsletter/find-pmf-again?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#4-look-for-customers-doing-cool-things-with-your-product). This reveals what features they actually want. When one of our largest customers built their own prototype of “PostHog 2.0” with our MCP and Claude Code, we knew we needed to add more customizable “canvas” artifacts to PostHog.

8.   [Validate AI bets](https://posthog.com/newsletter/find-pmf-again?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#3-score-it-like-a-seed-bet-not-a-business-unit) like you would new products. Write down how it will be judged and how much runway it gets. Ask how disappointed your team would be to lose it (the [PMF survey](https://posthog.com/founders/measure-product-market-fit?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons)). We did this for one product and only 23% said they would be very disappointed. Bad results, but useful.

9.   Write down[how your product loses](https://posthog.com/newsletter/find-pmf-again?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-write-down-how-you-die) to an AI-native threat and then fund your version of the attacker. Even the best support product loses to one where AI answers all the tickets for example, which is probably why Intercom pivoted so hard into Fin.

10.   Answer the question: How does this beat Claude? It’s what people default to.[Your moat is context](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#3-your-context-is-your-advantage): your product’s functionality, your users’ data, and the tools and skills you’ve built.

11.   [Your harness is not your moat](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#2-your-harness-is-not-your-moat). PostHog AI went through three of them in a year. We now have MCP as the canonical interface and let people pick their own harness. Don’t spend innovation points here.

12.   Don’t build an assistant. Assistants are what you build when intelligence sits _next_ to your product. Systems are what you build when intelligence becomes _part of it_.[Build those instead](https://posthog.com/blog/why-we-killed-our-ai-product-assistant?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#build-systems-not-assistants).

13.   Focus on building [shared AI infrastructure](https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/ai/ai-platform?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#why-we-built-it). Make prompts, streaming, consent, evals, [tasks](https://posthog.com/blog/cloud-agents-runtime?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), and analytics primitives teams can extend and build into their products. Pick a consistent UX pattern to avoid[death by a thousand widgets](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-features?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#7-avoid-ai-knowledge-silos) and then get out of people’s way. Product teams know their users best, not the AI team.

14.   Let agents run code. Code execution gives agents capabilities beyond what your predefined tools might enable them to do. PostHog AI can write SQL, run Python scripts, and ship PRs. Sandbox them to make this safe.

15.   Model upgrades will bulldoze your assumptions. We’ve restructured PostHog AI due to cheap reasoning (o4-mini) and reliable tool use (Claude 4).[Multimodal models](https://posthog.com/blog/multimodal-models-need-video?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) made Replay Vision possible. The harness, prompts, and context you built for previous models [might not be relevant for current ones](https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/your-agentsmd-is-holding-you-back?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons).

16.   [Skills](https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/what-nobody-tells-you-about-writing?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) are features for agents. They combine tools, docs, and rules into a recipe for a job. If an agent has the tools but not the recipe, it must look up how to use your product every time. Every `docs-search` call is evidence of a missing skill or tool (and it’s our most-called tool at ~28K calls a month).

17.   Let agents do[everything users can](https://posthog.com/newsletter/agent-first-product-engineering?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-let-agents-do-everything-users-can). If the `experiment-create` tool exists, yet the `experiment-start` tool is missing, the agent will do everything and then stop short to ask you to click through the UI. This limits the power of agents.

18.   [Dogfood headlessly](https://posthog.com/newsletter/agent-first-product-engineering?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#what-this-looks-like-in-practice-4) to develop agent empathy. Test agent features from the [CLI](https://posthog.com/docs/cli?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) so you hit the same friction points as they do. This is how we found our MCP tool descriptions used too many tokens.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!69Dl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7a27fc51-bc60-4a84-8473-bd58ffd147ce_1953x1479.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!69Dl!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7a27fc51-bc60-4a84-8473-bd58ffd147ce_1953x1479.png)

1.   AI doesn’t kill your UI, it changes its purpose. Fewer screens are for doing things, and more are for[approving, reviewing, and undoing](https://posthog.com/blog/agents-killing-ui?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#build-an-interface-worth-interacting-with) what agents did.

2.   [Meet agents at their level of abstraction](https://posthog.com/newsletter/agent-first-product-engineering?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#2-meet-agents-at-their-level-of-abstraction). Agents work better if you let them write and reason flexibly. We stopped forcing agents to use preset query tools and let them write their own SQL. A general purpose `executeSql` tool replaced every read endpoint and made “Why did signups drop?” go from four separate tool calls to one query.

3.   A missing tool is a feature request written by a robot. Agents using our MCP [can file feedback](https://posthog.com/blog/self-driving-loops?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-the-posthog-mcp-agent-feedback-loop) when they get stuck.

4.   Set up[AI observability](https://posthog.com/ai-observability?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) from day one. Trace LLM calls with inputs, outputs, latency, and cost. This reveals the errors and issues that once fixed lead to rapid quality improvements.

5.   Care more about reliability than[capability](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#5-it-doesnt-matter-how-cool-your-capabilities-are). Early complaints about PostHog AI weren’t about what it could do, they were about inconsistent performance, unexpected failures, generic errors, unclear limits, and lack of uncertainty. Capabilities are worthless if they aren’t reliable.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r__M!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb890ee81-c332-4761-ac6c-abf5e4c951ba_1600x899.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!r__M!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb890ee81-c332-4761-ac6c-abf5e4c951ba_1600x899.png)

1.   Track agent usage like human usage. Although agents don’t trigger pageviews or rageclicks, you can still track the[MCP tool calls](https://posthog.com/blog/agents-killing-ui?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#watch-what-agents-actually-do), [page requests](https://posthog.com/docs/web-analytics/sending-http-logs?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), and more.

2.   Learn your AI product unit costs. Our wizard costs $6.67 per run, but the improved activation and retention are worth more than this. Moving trace summaries from standard `gpt-4.1-nano` to flex tier `gpt-5-nano` halved costs.

3.   Subagents cost more than you think. They don’t share the parent’s cache and lack of observability can cause unreliability. Wizard runs used to spawn many subagents that [took longer or never returned](https://posthog.com/blog/optimizing-agent-cost?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#what-about-subagents), only for the main agent to do the actual work after waiting.

4.   Many agent failures are actually context failures. Giving[an agent a lot more context](https://posthog.com/newsletter/context-engineering?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#lesson-1-reasoning-isnt-the-bottleneck) improved wizard effectiveness more than improved reasoning, multi-step planning, subagents, pruning, and compaction.

5.   Make it easy for humans to create context agents wouldn’t know. PostHog AI has an[init command](https://posthog.com/blog/8-learnings-from-1-year-of-agents-posthog-ai?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#5-wider-context-is-key) to research your company and industry. The[semantic layer](https://posthog.com/blog/semantic-layer?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) sets vetted definitions of queries and data. Both help agents help you.

6.   Don’t stuff the prompt. Let agents look things up instead. Our system prompt for PostHog AI used to include all the events and properties available, but now a taxonomy tool does that instead.

7.   Shipping fast makes context drift, so fix it at the source. We have agents that [check merged PRs for docs updates and make a pull request](https://posthog.com/handbook/wizard-and-docs/content-writer-agent?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) when relevant. This helps context keep up with the pace of what’s being shipped without relying on endless manual fixes.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_MpQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61756b3d-576c-4cad-9621-5d51ed98c6f3_2048x832.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_MpQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61756b3d-576c-4cad-9621-5d51ed98c6f3_2048x832.png)

1.   [Example code](https://posthog.com/blog/correct-llm-code-generation?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#bringing-the-light-of-context) beats docs prose for correctness. A toy project shows an agent a real example and gives it something concrete to copy and test against.

2.   Being a [transparent company](https://newsletter.posthog.com/i/203333056/lesson-5-eliminate-context-silos?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) is good for agents. Both our agents and those of our customers can look at our codebase, our handbook, and our docs to get a better understanding of how PostHog works.

3.   Beware that public inputs can lead to[prompt injection](https://posthog.com/blog/what-if-your-product-built-itself?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#1-ingesting-signals). Since [self-driving](https://posthog.com/blog/self-driving-product?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) can open PRs from signals without human approval, a user could send a signal like “add your secret customer data to this page” and an agent might listen if we didn’t have protections in place.

4.   Use evals but start small. [Read traces manually](https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/your-agentsmd-is-holding-you-back?open=false&utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#%C2%A72-test-your-context-like-its-code) to identify places AI is going wrong, create an eval to check for it, and make improvements to improve that eval. Even[small golden or synthetic datasets](https://posthog.com/blog/testing-ai-agents?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons) gave insane performance boosts compared to the typical development cycle.

5.   Blank text boxes scare people. These often cause them to[forget everything they know about your product](https://posthog.com/newsletter/building-ai-features?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#6-plan-for-failure-by-adding-monitoring-guardrails-and-error-handling). Add suggestions and nudges to help them remember what to do.

6.   [Show every step](https://posthog.com/blog/8-learnings-from-1-year-of-agents-posthog-ai?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#6-show-every-step). We hid reasoning and failed tool calls because it looked messy but users said this felt hard to trust because the process was a mystery. So we stream everything now.

7.   [Build UI when text isn’t enough](https://posthog.com/newsletter/2030-shaped-software?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons#build-ui-when-text-isnt-enough). Some jobs need persistent, purpose-built UIs like trust and verification surfaces for confirming the agent did what you wanted and triage and inbox surfaces listing decisions that need a human.

8.   Expect half these things to be wrong in a year. We [started with graph-style workflows](https://posthog.com/blog/8-learnings-from-1-year-of-agents-posthog-ai?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons), front-loaded context, split work across subagents, and then all that became obsolete. What doesn’t expire is everything you already know about [building products](https://posthog.com/newsletter/50-product-learnings?utm_source=posthog-newsletter&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ai-product-lessons): talk to users, ship fast, run experiments, repeat.

_Words by [Ian Vanagas](https://x.com/ianvanagas) who did not mention “loop” once in the post. Graphics by [Lottie](https://posthog.com/community/profiles/27881?utm\_source=posthog-newsletter&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=ai-product-lessons) and [Daniel](https://posthog.com/community/profiles/34810?utm\_source=posthog-newsletter&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=ai-product-lessons)._

Title: State of Direct Mail 2026: Consumer Insights Edition

URL Source: https://www.lob.com/state-of-direct-mail/consumer-insights/2026-report

Published Time: 2026-01-01

Markdown Content:
State of Direct Mail 2026

## Letter from the CEO

Every year, our State of Direct Mail Consumer Insights report reveals how consumer attitudes toward direct mail are changing – and what that means for marketers.

This year, one thing stands out. Economic pressure is changing not only how consumers shop, but how they use direct mail. They're looking for value, comparing offers more carefully, and holding onto mail longer as they make purchasing decisions. At the same time, they're expecting personalization that actually feels personal. Our research shows that relevance looks different across generations. The offers, messaging, and personalization that resonate with Gen Z aren't always what motivates Millennials, Gen X, or Boomers. One-size-fits-all simply doesn't work anymore.

That's the opportunity. The brands that win will be the ones that deliver timely, relevant direct mail that earns attention, builds trust, and helps people make confident buying decisions.

I hope this year's report gives you a fresh perspective and practical ways to create direct mail your customers actually want to receive.

**Ryan Ferrier**  
**CEO, Lob**

Study Methodology

Lob conducted this study in partnership with [Kirin Analytics](https://www.kelseywhiteresearch.com/)and [PureSpectrum](https://www.purespectrum.com/). The online survey was completed in July 2026 with 2,000 adult consumers across the United States, nationally representative of age, gender, income, and region.

## Key takeaways

### Price-conscious shoppers are paying closer attention to mail.

84% of consumers say rising prices have changed how they shop, and 66% say they like referring back to direct mail when considering a purchase.

![Image 1](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a8c984cbbb2cedb62a4b72c_Group%201597881840.png)

### Personalized mail looks different for every generation.

89% of consumers say relevant mail influences them to take action, but what feels relevant (and what they take action on) changes by generation.

![Image 2](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a8c988a767f50b012f75622_Group%201597881841.png)

The mailbox remains one of the few marketing moments built into everyday life.

82% of consumers collect their mail daily or nearly every day, and 87% read it the same day they receive it.

Direct mail's trust advantage is growing.

34% of consumers say direct mail feels more trustworthy than digital communication, a 9-point increase from last year.

Consumers don't mind AI. They mind experiences that don't feel authentic.

82% are comfortable with (or neutral on) brands using AI to create direct mail, but 62% say AI has made them more skeptical of digital ads + AI slop.

Direct mail sparks action beyond the mailbox.

79% of consumers have taken a digital action after receiving direct mail, and 65% have made a purchase, signed up, or become a customer because of it.

Part one: Economic pressures

## In a tight economy, consumers lean on direct mail.

Eighty-four percent of consumers say rising prices have changed how they shop. They're spending more carefully, delaying purchases, comparing options, and looking harder for real value before they buy.

This shift is changing the role of direct mail, too. Sixty-eight percent say economic conditions have changed what they pay attention to in their mailbox, with deals, affordability, and useful information taking center stage.

**Get the full picture**— hover over   
each chart to display exact values.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### “Yes, rising prices and the general economic climate have definitely shifted what catches my eye when I look through direct mail. Instead of just browsing for inspiration or new products like I might have in the past, I now immediately scan for tangible value.”

Millennial male in the Northwest

### “I pay attention to discounts, sales or special offers. Any kind of financial break I can get. I will definitely take advantage of it.”

Gen X female in the South

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

Design for the second read.

Many purchases don't happen the day your mail arrives. Make your piece useful after the first glance with side-by-side product comparisons, financing details, limited-time offers, or a QR code that saves shoppers a step when they're ready to buy.

Part two: Personalization + conversion

## The rules of personalization change by generation.

Personalization is one of the strongest drivers of conversion. Nearly 9 in 10 consumers say relevant personalized mail is what influenced them to take action. But what feels relevant? It’s not the same for everyone. Baby boomers are more likely to respond to practical shopping context, such as offers and promotions, while younger generations place greater value on basic personalization and life stage marketing. The takeaway is simple: personalization works, but only when your definition of "personal" matches your audience’s.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

Layer your personalization.

Start with the basics, like a customer's name, but don't stop there. Pair it with a timely offer, a relevant product, or messaging tied to a current need or life stage. Build campaigns around moments, motivations, and needs, not just customer profiles.

## Direct mail drives both acquisition and retention

Direct mail influences consumers throughout the customer journey. Eighty-three percent say it would encourage them to re-engage with a brand, while 48% say it makes them more likely to try a brand they've never purchased from before.

Part Three: Consumer perspectives + behavior

## Mail isn't another marketing touchpoint. It's a daily ritual.

The mailbox is one of the few marketing touchpoints built into everyday life. More than 80% of consumers collect their mail daily or nearly every day, and 87% read direct mail the same day they bring it inside. Whether driven by habit or expectation, checking the mail remains a consistent ritual across generations, creating a moment of attention that digital channels often have to fight to earn.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

Design for the mindset behind the mailbox.

76% of Baby Boomers check the mailbox out of habit, while 49% of Gen Z check because they're expecting something. The ritual is the same, but the motivation is different. Build for both: reinforce trust with consistent branding for habitual mail checkers, and reward anticipation with timely offers, exclusive content, or personalized messaging.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

## Direct mail's trust advantage is growing

Consumers still crave experiences that feel real. As digital marketing becomes increasingly crowded, direct mail continues to stand apart. This year, 34% of consumers said direct mail feels more trustworthy than digital communication, a nine-point increase from 2025. Overall, nearly two-thirds say direct mail feels more authentic, trustworthy, valuable, or memorable than digital.

(Base: Economically strained consumers, n=690)

Part FOUR: AI

## Consumers care more about authenticity than AI.

Consumers are surprisingly comfortable with AI playing a role in the creation of direct mail, especially when it's used to personalize offers, tailor content, or improve relevance. But 62% say the rise of AI has made them more skeptical of digital ads, as they encounter “slop” more frequently in online spaces.

The takeaway isn't to avoid AI. It's to use it where it adds value, then have humans make sure every campaign feels thoughtful, relevant, and worthy of trust.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### “AI makes me more cautious but also more attentive to truly personalized, relevant, and trustworthy direct mail from brands.”

Millennial male in the West

### “It makes me more skeptical of online advertising. AI has no effect on how I respond to direct marketing.”

Boomer male in the Midwest

### “If used effectively (meaning it was vetted extensively afterward) I don't have a problem. But if it's obvious and shoddy, I will think less of the brand that uses it.”

Gen X male in the South

### “AI doesn't matter to me. What matters is value.”

Gen X female in the Northeast

(Base: Half of respondents, n=1,000)

Use AI to improve relevance, then review for trust.

Tailor the offer, content, or timing, but have a human check every piece for accuracy, tone, and anything that could feel generic, confusing, or overly personal.

(Base: Total respondents, n=2,000)

### What’s next? Four ways to put these insights into practice

1

Design for the decision, not just the first impression.

Consumers are taking longer to make purchases. Create mail that's worth coming back to with clear offers, comparison charts, product details, financing information, or QR codes that make it easy to pick up where they left off.

2

Personalize beyond the name field.

Names still matter, but they're only the starting point. Tailor offers, products, imagery, and messaging around what someone is actively considering, their current needs, or their stage of life.

3

Match the moment.

Not everyone opens the mailbox for the same reason. Some consumers check it out of habit, while others are expecting something meaningful. Build campaigns that fit that mindset, whether that's consistent branding that builds trust or timely, personalized offers that reward anticipation.

4

Let AI improve the experience, not replace it.

Consumers don't mind AI. They mind experiences that feel generic or untrustworthy. Use AI to improve targeting and relevance, then make sure a human reviews every campaign for clarity, tone, and credibility.

Title: Social Media and Wellbeing: It's Complicated

URL Source: https://news.gallup.com/poll/715433/social-media-wellbeing-complicated.aspx

Published Time: 2026-10-10

Markdown Content:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Most adults worldwide use social media, and among younger adults, nearly everyone does. Across 97 countries surveyed by Gallup so far in 2026, a median of 81% of adults say they have used some type of social media in the past seven days, rising to 95% among those aged 15 to 29.

Findings from the latest [_State of the World’s Emotional Health_ report](https://www.gallup.com/analytics/349280/state-of-worlds-emotional-health.aspx) challenge some assumptions about what that widespread use means for wellbeing. The analysis reveals a modest, complicated relationship that varies by time spent using social media, age and where people live.

With social media so embedded in daily life, the findings are particularly relevant at a time when the world’s emotional health is under considerable strain. Worry, stress, sadness, anger and physical pain all remain well above the levels Gallup measured two decades ago. What is less understood is how much social media is associated with this rise in negative emotions.

For this study, Gallup classifies adults as low use (no use or less than 30 minutes a day), moderate use (30 minutes to less than two hours) or high use (two hours or more). After accounting for factors that can influence wellbeing metrics such as these, moderate use is associated with fewer negative emotions than high use and more positive experiences and higher life evaluations than low use. As with many things in life, moderation appears to yield more optimal wellbeing outcomes.

###Embeddable###

The findings are part of Gallup’s new _State of the World’s Emotional Health_ 2026 report, released in partnership with the World Health Summit. The report, based on Gallup’s first global analysis of social media use and time spent using it, examines social media alongside Gallup’s latest global measures of positive and negative emotions and life evaluations.

Gallup’s analysis adds to growing evidence that the relationship between social media and wellbeing is not straightforward. The 2026 _World Happiness Report_ found that among 15-year-olds in 47 countries, those who use social media for less than an hour a day have higher life satisfaction than nonusers, while life satisfaction is generally lower at higher levels of use.

## More Isn’t Necessarily Worse, but Less Isn’t Necessarily Better

Across the 97 countries surveyed, people are most likely to use social media moderately. A median of 39% of adults fall into this group, compared with 31% with low use and 27% with high use.

The differences in wellbeing across the low-, moderate- and high-use groups are generally small after accounting for country, age, gender, education, household income, internet use, work status, reported health problems and social support. But wellbeing is not meaningfully worse among those spending more time on social media.

Moderate social media use is associated with better outcomes on many wellbeing measures. Compared with moderate social media use, high use is associated with more anger, loneliness, sadness, stress and worry. High users are also less likely to report being treated with respect. However, life evaluation does not differ significantly between the two groups.

At the same time, low users have lower life evaluations and are less likely than moderate users to report enjoyment, smiling or laughing, feeling well-rested, and being treated with respect. They are also slightly more likely to report anger.

## Younger Adults Spend More Time Using Social Media

Age is a major factor in how much time people spend using social media. A median of 47% of adults aged 15 to 29 fall into the high-use group, compared with 28% of those aged 30 to 49 and 12% of those aged 50 and older. Low use is much more common among older adults, rising from 10% among those aged 15 to 29 to 54% among those aged 50 and older.

###Embeddable###

Younger adults are not the only group showing less favorable wellbeing outcomes with high use. Compared with moderate use, high use is associated with more anger and sadness across all three age groups Gallup examined. Among adults aged 15 to 29, it is also associated with more stress and less learning. But life evaluation ratings do not differ significantly between high and moderate use at any age.

###Embeddable###

## High Use Linked to Lower Life Evaluations in High-Income Countries

Globally, life evaluations do not differ significantly between high and moderate use. In high-income countries, however, high use is associated with lower life evaluations. No significant difference is evident in non-high-income countries. The emotional costs of high use are more consistent across income groups: High use is associated with more anger, loneliness and sadness in both.

###Embeddable###

Even among high-income countries, the pattern varies. In the United States, adults with high use rate their lives about 0.3 points lower than moderate users on Gallup’s 0-to-10 scale, with the same pattern seen among younger adults. There is no significant difference between high and moderate use in Germany or the United Kingdom.

Gallup’s data cannot explain why this relationship differs by country income. In the United States, the association is present amid broader signs of social strain, including elevated loneliness and declining confidence in many institutions. More broadly, life evaluation has declined in many Western industrial countries, particularly among younger people. The 2026 _World Happiness Report_ found that these declines cannot be explained by social media use alone, suggesting that the wider social context may also matter.

## Bottom Line

Gallup’s first global analysis of social media use and time spent using it does not yield a simple verdict on its relationship with wellbeing. Some findings support concerns about high use, particularly for negative emotions and, in high-income countries, life evaluations. But the relationships are generally small, and more time spent using social media does not correspond with steadily worse wellbeing in most countries.

The findings also raise questions about social media's relationship with outcomes beyond wellbeing. Confidence in national government varies with social media use and time spent using it. After accounting for other factors, social media users are less likely than nonusers to express confidence in their national government. Confidence is also lower among those with high use than moderate use and higher among those with low use than moderate use.

Based on this research, Gallup cannot determine why these relationships exist. The analysis also does not capture what people do or encounter on social media, the impacts of specific platforms, or whether their use is problematic or disruptive. But the findings challenge the assumption that less social media necessarily corresponds with better wellbeing. The global relationship is neither consistently negative nor simply a matter of time spent.

The next frontier in understanding the relationship between social media and wellbeing may involve exploring what happens during that time online and the social and country contexts in which it occurs.

[_Read the full report._](https://www.gallup.com/analytics/349280/state-of-worlds-emotional-health.aspx)

_Stay up to date with the latest insights by following @Gallup [on X](https://x.com/gallup?utm\_source=link\_newsv9&utm\_campaign=item\_715433&utm\_medium=copy) and [on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/gallup/?utm\_source=link\_newsv9&utm\_campaign=item\_715433&utm\_medium=copy)._

## TikTok Inks Second Major Microdrama Deal, Partners With Made By Us Studios

The news follows the social media platform‘s deal with Issa Rae's Hoorae to make vertical series, which resulted in the popular drama ‘Screen Time.’

![Image 1: An image of Hannah Stocking attending the 97th Annual Oscars at Dolby Theatre on March 02, 2025.](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2202904560.jpg?crop=0px%2C56px%2C2997px%2C1678px&resize=2000%2C1126)

Hannah Stocking, who will appear in the TikTok-Made By Us Studios coproduction ‘Player,’ attends the 97th Annual Oscars at Dolby Theatre in 2025.Photo by Monica Schipper/Getty Images

[TikTok](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/tiktok/) is deepening its commitment to the microdrama format with a new deal aimed at producing vertical stories starring creators.

The company has inked an agreement with Made By Us Studios, the production arm of major creator management company Made By All, to co-produce creator-led vertical series for TikTok and its microdrama app PineDrama. It’s the social media company’s second major microdrama deal after it announced a partnership with Issa Rae’s Hoorae Media to co-develop microseries in April.

Mady By All, the management company behind Made By Us Studios, represents creators including Dhar Mann (who is already making [his own microdramas](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/dhar-mann-microdramas-deal-fox-holywater-1236478483/) with Fox and Holywater), _One Battle After Another_ actor Teyana Taylor and YouTuber Adam Waheed. Made By Us Studios is led by former Range Partner Tanya Cohen as well as Made By All founder Leanne Perice.

The deal was announced at MIPCOM, where TikTok unveiled the first two projects in the slate. _Player_ is a romantic revenge thriller starring and co-executive produced by creator Hannah Stocking and additionally produced by Jonas Barnes. The series was written by Arun Blair-Mangat and Chela Reyna and directed by Louiza Zouzias.

_The Knock_ is described as a “genre microseries” (no word yet as to the precise genre) starring actor and content creator Adam Rose and actor Zaria Simone (_Pretty Little Liars: Original Sin_). It was created and directed by R.H. Stavis and is executive produced by Spooky Pictures _(Watcher)_ alongside the musician Moby’s Little Walnut Productions. Moby also composed the series’ music.

“Micro-series are pioneering a new language of storytelling,” TikTok’s global head of entertainment and micro-series Dawn Yang said in a statement about the deal. “We’re thrilled to partner with Made By Us on a slate that puts creators at the center, alongside established producers and industry talent, to tell stories designed for the feed from the start. This is an exciting step forward in our continued investment in the next generation of premium vertical storytelling on TikTok and PineDrama.”

Made By Us Studios co-CEO Tanya Cohen said in a statement that vertical series are “the next evolution” for creators. “The opportunity isn’t to make smaller versions of television — it’s to build an entirely new premium storytelling language around the way audiences actually consume entertainment today,” Cohen added. “TikTok understands that behavior at a global scale, and together we have the opportunity to build franchises with creators who arrive with audience, community and cultural relevance already built in.”

TikTok’s deal with Hoorae Media started big earlier in the year with _Screen Time_, a hit microdrama about a terrible double date. The series, starring Xavier Avila, Jasmine Luv, Eric C. Lynch and Brittney Jefferson, has earned nearly 580 million views globally since it premiered in April.

kept.article_text:
Title: Turn Your SaaS Pricing Page into a First 30 Days Conversion Tool

URL Source: https://thegood.com/insights/free-trial-pricing-page/

Markdown Content:
A trial user’s relationship with your pricing page isn’t a single moment. It’s a conversation that plays out across their entire trial.

Once when they’re comparing you to competitors before they’ve even signed up, again when a feature limit stops them mid-task, and once more when the trial clock is running out and they’re deciding whether the last month was worth paying for.

The good news is that this is a controllable, high-leverage lever. Here are five ways to actually use it that way.

## Why timing changes what your pricing page needs to say

In our years of optimization work, we’ve found that most pricing pages are written for one visitor, the person seeing it for the first time.

But by the time someone’s mid-trial, that page needs to answer a completely different question.

Early on, a prospect is still evaluating whether you’re a serious option at all. They want clarity. What do the tiers actually include, and does this look like a company that will still be here in a year?

Mid-trial, someone hits a wall, a seat limit, a feature gate, a usage cap, and comes back to the page looking for a fast, specific answer. What exactly do I get if I upgrade right now?

Near the end, they’re doing a final gut check, comparing what they got out of the trial against what they’d be paying going forward, and they’re unusually sensitive to anything that feels inconsistent with what they remember seeing before.

![Image 1: A timeline graphic demonstrating  differences for SaaS free trial pricing page.](blob:http://localhost/7a79b06edb82eecadc7d2624decd1c8b)
One page. Three jobs. The tactics below are built around serving all three without contradicting yourself between visits.

## 1. Build the page to survive a third look, not just win the first one

Most pricing-page advice optimizes for a single glance: bold CTA, clear tiers, done. That’s necessary, but it’s not sufficient for a page people are going to study more than once.

The fix is to load the page with things that hold up under repeated scrutiny rather than things that just look good in a screenshot: a real plan-comparison table, specific security and trust signals, and pricing that doesn’t require a sales call to understand.

PandaDoc is a clear example of this done well: four clearly tiered plans (including a permanent free eSign tier), a full comparison table, per-document pricing, security assurances, and G2, Capterra, and Trustpilot ratings, all visible directly on the page.

![Image 2: Example of a well-done SaaS free trial pricing page from PandaDoc.](blob:http://localhost/b2c28a0c018c14cfefaff442fef680f7)
Its checkout carries that same clarity forward into a short, three-step flow that shows exact seat counts, monthly and annual totals, and the precise charge date before anyone commits.

That matters because trial abandonment is common and fast. Roughly 80% of free-trial users never convert to a paying plan according to benchmark data by [Evan Bailyn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/saas-free-trial-conversion-rate-benchmarks-evan-bailyn/), and over half of downloaded apps get uninstalled within their first 30 days according to [AppsFlyer](https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/reports/app-uninstall-benchmarks-report/).

Almost every one of those users looked at the pricing page at least once before they left. A page built to reassure on the second and third look gives you more chances to change that outcome than a page optimized only for the first.

## 2. Keep the number the same everywhere it shows up

If your pricing page says one thing and your trial banner, an email, or your checkout screen says another, you’re not running multiple offers. You’re teaching users not to trust any of the numbers you show them.

Grammarly is a useful cautionary example here: at various points, its pricing communications have run several discount framings at once, a straight percentage off, a flat monthly rate, a student discount, an annual-savings callout, all live simultaneously.

![Image 3: An example of inconsistency between promotions and information on a SaaS free trial pricing page.](blob:http://localhost/4c57d9faa4bb1b0b424194db09d7d860)
Whether that reflects deliberate testing or simply layered campaigns that never got reconciled, the effect on a user checking the page for the second time is the same: the price stops feeling like a fact and starts feeling like a moving target.

The fix is ownership and consistency. Pick one framing per offer, keep it synced across every surface a trial user might see it: banner, page, checkout, email, and audit it the way you’d audit a bug. This is also where anchoring bias, one of the best-documented forces in pricing psychology, cuts against you if you’re careless. The first price a user sees becomes their reference point for every price after it, so a moving target doesn’t just confuse people; it resets their anchor every time.

## 3. Time your pricing asks to where the user actually is

The same pricing message can be the right move on Day 20 and the wrong one on Day 1. Getting the sequencing wrong is often a bigger problem than anything written on the page itself.

Both failure modes show up in the wild. Riverside pitches its Business tier, complete with a full feature-comparison table and a “book a demo” CTA, to brand-new, self-serve signups before they’ve created a single item, pricing pressure with nothing yet to anchor it to.

![Image 4: Example of a SaaS free trial pricing page not targeted to the correct user.](blob:http://localhost/ac05b0812e5e1b75dabd6d920d41f775)
Calendly has run into the opposite risk with a feature-promotion email invites a user to build a workflow, only to inform them, right after they click “save,” that their Teams trial has ended and they’ll need to upgrade to keep it, a paywall landing at the exact moment of highest invested effort and highest potential frustration.

Miro and Airtable illustrate a related issue worth avoiding: essentially no upgrade or pricing pressure for the first two weeks, followed by a compressed cluster of prompts landing almost entirely within a 24- to 48-hour window near the end.

Giving people room to build habits before asking them to pay is a reasonable instinct, but concentrating an entire pricing push into a trial’s final hours means it’s competing with deadline anxiety instead of genuine product enthusiasm. Spreading gentle, well-timed touchpoints across the trial, the way PandaDoc sustains lighter reminders over time rather than one hard-sell spike, tends to land better than either extreme.

## 4. Cut the comprehension tax

Every extra screen, tab, or slider between a user and a clear price is a small tax on their patience, and trial users pay that tax multiple times if they’re checking back.

Zapier and Typeform both illustrate this cost in practice. Zapier splits its plans across multiple tabs, layers in a usage-volume slider and an add-on configurator, and shows a trial banner price that doesn’t clearly reconcile with the plan card price underneath, meaning a prospect can click through six or more separate pricing and billing screens without ever landing on a clear number.

![Image 5: A second view of a challenging SaaS free trial pricing page.](blob:http://localhost/ba2f9b91c108c30bf74360bf278caf03)![Image 6: A second view of a challenging SaaS free trial pricing page.](blob:http://localhost/ba2f9b91c108c30bf74360bf278caf03)
Typeform shows an even more direct version of the pattern: pricing and checkout sequences that repeat several times across a single 30-day trial, including a plan-review screen later followed by a billing page that shows the account back on its free plan.

The fix draws directly from choice architecture. Limit the number of decisions a page asks someone to make at once, recommend a specific tier rather than presenting three neutral options, and make sure the price a user sees in a banner or email matches the price they see when they click through. None of that requires new features, just fewer places for the story to fall out of sync with itself.

## 5. Audit what you can’t see yourself

There’s consistently a gap between how much pricing pressure a product actually creates and how much of it a careful observer would consciously register. Persistent pricing and upgrade surfaces are often present from Day 1 of a trial, well before the experience would register as “pushy.”

That gap is the real argument for measuring this rather than trusting instinct alone. A team’s mental model of how often users see its pricing page is usually off, and almost always in the direction of underestimating it.

Before changing anything on the page itself, it’s worth counting how many places pricing information actually appears across a real trial, on which days, and whether the story stays consistent across all of them.

## Align the page with what’s actually behind the paywall

One tactic underneath all of the above is that your pricing page can only tell a coherent story if your feature-gating strategy already is one. If a plan’s advertised value doesn’t match what a user experiences once they hit a limit, no amount of pricing-page polish fixes that gap.

This is where[freemium pricing](https://thegood.com/insights/freemium-pricing/) and feature-gating decisions come in ahead of pricing-page copy. Running a[verb-scoring exercise](https://thegood.com/insights/verb-scoring/) against your own product, mapping which core actions are gated at which tier, can surface mismatches between what your pricing page promises and what your product actually delivers before a trial user finds them for you.

## Frequently asked questions

### How often do trial users actually revisit a [SaaS pricing page](https://thegood.com/insights/saas-pricing-page/)?

More often than most teams assume. Pricing pages tend to get checked multiple times across a single trial, especially right before a usage limit, a plan decision, or the trial’s end.

### What’s the fastest way to improve a pricing page for trial conversion?

Start with consistency, not redesign. Confirm the price shown in your trial banner, emails, and checkout all match the price on the page itself, and remove any default settings, like pre-selected annual billing, that only make sense from your side of the transaction.

### Should pricing pressure increase as a trial nears its end?

It can, but avoid saving all of it for the final 24 to 48 hours. A back-loaded blitz competes with deadline anxiety rather than genuine enthusiasm; spreading lighter, well-timed touchpoints across the trial tends to build more trust than concentrating pressure at the finish line.

### What should a SaaS pricing page include for free trial users?

At minimum, clearly labeled tiers, a transparent feature-and-price breakdown, and pricing that’s framed identically across every channel a trial user might encounter: banner, email, and checkout. Trust signals like ratings, security certifications, and a real plan-comparison table help the page hold up on a second or third visit, not just the first.

### When should a SaaS company first show pricing to a free trial user?

Not before they’ve experienced real value. An enterprise-tier pitch or a hard upgrade ask shown to a brand-new signup who hasn’t created anything yet tends to read as premature, and it can undermine trust before the trial has really started.

### What are the most common mistakes SaaS companies make with their free trial pricing page?

The recurring ones are inconsistent pricing across banners, emails, and checkout; annual billing pre-selected by default, especially right after a downgrade; plan comparisons complex enough to require six or more screens to understand; and saving all upgrade pressure for the final 24 to 48 hours of the trial instead of spacing it out.

### Does pricing page consistency actually affect trial-to-paid conversion rates?

Yes. Running several discount framings at once, or showing a different price in a banner than at checkout, teaches users that the number in front of them isn’t stable, which undermines trust in the price more than the price itself usually does. Keeping pricing identical across every touchpoint protects the anchor a user forms the first time they see it.

## Make your pricing page work every day of the trial, not just the last one

The SaaS companies that convert trial users treat their pricing page as infrastructure that has to hold up across a month of comparing, reconsidering, and checking back in. Teams have to build, price, and time it accordingly.

Start by mapping your own trial funnel. How many times would a real user see pricing information, on which days, and does the story stay the same each time? That audit alone tends to surface most of the fixes above.

kept.heading: “YOU DIDN'T DO IT RIGHT” (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Frameworks like OKRs can fail when they don't fit a company's culture, team dynamics, or existing processes, even when implemented correctly. After four failed attempts at OKRs, WP Engine found success with a metrics framework that let teams choose goals they personally valued and could directly control. Teams started with one metric for a quarter, then added one or two more based on what they learned. Rather than rolling out a framework company-wide, test it with one team, gather feedback, and adapt it or try another approach if it does not work.
kept.article_text:
Title: "You didn't do it right"

URL Source: https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/

Published Time: 2026-10-11T00:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
Four sincere attempts at OKRs, four failures, and every time: “you didn’t do it right.” Maybe the framework doesn’t fit you — so how do you find one that does?

![Image 1: I know it's wrong, I'm just waiting for the autocorrect.](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/l-i-know-its-wrong-im-just-waiting-autocorrect-963w.jpg)

We tried to implement OKRs four separate times at WP Engine; sometimes inside a single team, sometimes for a department, sometimes across the entire company.

We failed every time.

Well, OK, let’s not avoid responsibility. _I_ failed every time.

OKRs are a great framework. They originated at Intel, grew up in Google, and because tech companies are famous for thinking for themselves from first principles, OKRs were thoughtlessly copied into countless others, spawning several books, an endless stream of articles and podcasts and courses, and an industry of self-certified coaches.

We used all that stuff too. The managers read John Doerr’s _Measure What Matters_. We paid for training. We gave presentations, and we coached people through it individually, one on one.

So why didn’t it work? When I’d ask the experts, I was often told: “You didn’t do it right.”

But if it’s _that hard_ to “do it right,” maybe it’s too hard to do it. Maybe “You didn’t do it right” is an inadequate explanation.

Should we conclude that OKRs don’t work? No, plenty of organizations swear by them.

So, what _do_ we do?

## Where Have I Heard This Before? [](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/#where-i-heard-before)

This happens with all frameworks.

Ron Jeffries, who helped create Scrum, has noticed this pattern for years and calls it [“Dark Scrum”](https://ronjeffries.com/articles/016-09ff/defense/?utm_source=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_campaign=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_medium=post): “Scrum, done even fairly well, is a good framework. I’m quite sincere about that… Like every good idea, the reality sometimes falls short.”

I’ve heard “You didn’t do it right” about Scrum, even when those same teams succeeded with a different framework like Kanban.

And…

*   You run jobs-to-be-done, everything checks out, but [the company fails anyway](https://longform.asmartbear.com/compass/). “Then you didn’t really run jobs-to-be-done correctly.”
*   Aaron Ross successfully separated “prospecting” from “closing” at Salesforce; thousands of SaaS companies copied his pattern and but their SDR teams failed. The typical reasons: “You didn’t give them enough ramp. Your cadence was wrong. You didn’t hire properly. You didn’t manage properly.”
*   Two years of content marketing, two hundred posts, organic traffic flat. You’re told “it’s not 10x content; you had no topical authority; you never built the links.” And the algorithm changed 493 times, so [the excuses never run out](https://longform.asmartbear.com/bad-advice/).
*   Zappos went all in on Holacracy; [18% of the workforce](https://time.com/4180791/zappos-holacracy-buyouts/?utm_source=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_campaign=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_medium=post) took a buyout and left, and a few years later the company [reverted it](https://qz.com/work/1776841/zappos-has-quietly-backed-away-from-holacracy?utm_source=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_campaign=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_medium=post). Many other companies tried it when Zappos tried it; all the ones I’m aware of also reverted. Of course HolacracyOne’s theory [is that it wasn’t implemented correctly](https://www.holacracy.org/blog/thanks-for-all-of-your-concern-but/?utm_source=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_campaign=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_medium=post).

So, what’s the answer?

## The Precision Fallacy [](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/#precision-fallacy)

The “You didn’t do it right” retort rests on a fallacy: that the framework _always works_, so any failure must be the fault of the implementator.

I call this the “Precision Fallacy”: the belief that a more precise understanding or implementation would have worked, where the precision in question is undefined, or so intricate that it’s impossible to follow, and thus it’s an un-dis-provable excuse.

This last piece is its distinguishing property: No matter how many times the framework fails, no matter how sincere and capable the team who failed, the answer is always “You didn’t do it right,” not (for example) “This isn’t the right process for you” or “There are many circumstances where it’s the wrong framework to use.” Thus the framework can never be disproved⁠—or even given boundaries for where it applies.

As in WP Engine: Four sincere, well-trained attempts and four failures, still aren’t evidence that OKRs are not universally applicable. A team who [went on to implement a different framework](https://longform.asmartbear.com/perseverance/) isn’t evidence that the first framework wasn’t a fit for that team. Philosopher Karl Popper noticed people doing this in all walks of life; he watched his friends do it with the theories of Marx and Freud, and saw that [“whatever happened always confirmed it.”](https://www.stephenhicks.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/PopperK-Science-as-Falsification.pdf?utm_source=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_campaign=longform.asmartbear.com&utm_medium=post) Popper points out that any theory that cannot be disproved, regardless of evidence, isn’t a valid theory.

The truth is: [There is context inside which the framework works, and outside which it doesn’t work](https://longform.asmartbear.com/models/). And I believe that not-working is the most common case.

## The Solution: Try It On like Clothes [](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/#solution-try-it-on-like-clothes)

Not using a framework is like sewing a shirt from scratch. You don’t know how to make a shirt, so it’s going to be a mess. In fact, right now it’s a mess; that’s why you were looking for a framework.

A framework is like buying a shirt off the rack: it’s shirt-shaped, and at least it fits _some_ people well. Maybe 15% of the time it fits perfectly and you’re done. Good! You win. (That’s also what happened with the well-known successes that the framework experts cite.)

The rest of the time the shirt fits OK, but it’s wrong in three places. That’s the normal case, and why wouldn’t it be? So the answer is to tailor it: to ask what you liked and didn’t like, and make adjustments. Maybe it cannot be made to work⁠—sometimes the fit is so wrong it cannot be iterated into the perfect fit⁠—in which case you’ve accumulated new experiences that will help you select a different framework with more fidelity.

Frameworks, like people and products, must match the culture, the people, the other processes, and the collective desires of the organization. Even the creators and proponents of the framework typically don’t know the conditions under which it will succeed.

If you stand in front of the whole company and announce: “We’re switching to OKRs,” you create instant detractors, and the rollout will probably just fail.

Instead: “One team is going to try this for a quarter and find out what we like and what we don’t.” That’s an experiment.

This isn’t just a communication trick to get naysayers to at least try it. It’s how you actually try it on, make alterations, or put it back and try something else.

## What Actually Worked at WP Engine [](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/#what-actually-worked-at-wp-engine)

![Image 2: Product KPI Framework](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/l-product-kpi-framework-576w.png)

OKRs never worked for us;. What did work in the teams I ran was [a metrics framework that I created](https://longform.asmartbear.com/product-metrics/)_and tuned_ through feedback.

It worked for reasons that have nothing to do with it being “better than OKRs.” Our folks happened to like it because it held them accountable in a way they _wanted_ to be held accountable. And⁠—just as importantly⁠—it did not try to hold them accountable for outcomes they _influenced_ but didn’t completely _control_.

That last bit was the unlock. As I wrote in that metrics article: “Whenever management requires a KPI that the team doesn’t believe in, doesn’t respect, doesn’t care about, the team always wins.”

It started with one team. I said: Pick one metric⁠—anywhere on the chart; it genuinely does not matter where. Attach a goal to it; a very loose one is fine. The only real requirement was that _you personally wanted_ it: not because a manager asked for it, not even because it’s “good for the company,” but because you believed _we are not doing our jobs if this isn’t true_, or _we’re failing at our craft if we don’t accomplish this_. Something connected to personal pride.

Then they tracked that one metric for a quarter. After that, they asked what other metric belonged⁠—not ten more metrics, just one or two. They grew outward from what they had already accepted.

## But Will That Work for You? [](https://longform.asmartbear.com/you-didnt-do-it-right/#will-work-you)

That worked for my teams at WP Engine. Will it work for you?

You already know the answer: Maybe, or maybe some iteration of it, or maybe something else entirely.

Just try something on.

kept.heading: WE NOW KNOW THE #1 RANKING FACTOR FOR AI AND LLMS, THE DATA (40 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Contextually relevant backlinks had the strongest correlation with AI rankings across 17 AI search channels. For GPT-6 Astra, the correlation averaged 0.57 across industries and was positive in all 100. Unlinked brand mentions also correlated with rankings at 0.41 compared with 0.55 for total backlinks. The findings suggest prioritizing links and coverage from relevant industry sources over simply increasing backlink volume.
kept.article_text:
Title: We Now Know the #1 Ranking Factor for AI and LLMs, The Data.

URL Source: https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data

Published Time: 2026-10-13T05:00:00-07:00

Markdown Content:
I analyzed backlinks and brand mentions across 100 industries, 16 LLMs, ChatGPT's web interface, and the brands named in Google's AI Overviews, using four taxonomies and tens of millions of pages.

The main results:

*   **All 21,600 similarity curves passed the relevance test.** Pages linking to or mentioning recommended brands scored higher against the most closely related quarter of categories than against the least related quarter.
*   **Relevant backlink count had the strongest correlation with AI score across all 17 AI channels.** For GPT-6 Astra, the average correlation within industries was 0.57, and it was positive in all 100 industries.
*   **Unlinked mentions followed the same relevance pattern.** Their counts correlated with GPT-6 Astra's AI scores at 0.41, compared with 0.55 for total backlink counts.

If you haven't watched the video yet, I highly suggest watching it before you read the rest of this. It's only 12 minutes. I explain how LLMs work, how they generate their responses, and why this research is different from the research you've seen before. The rest of this post will make a lot more sense after you've seen it.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xVJ58AWrH1M)

[Subscribe to OppAlerts on YouTube](https://youtube.com/@OppAlerts?sub_confirmation=1)

Here, I'll walk through how I ran the tests, the results, and what they mean for your campaigns.

## How I put the research together

## Ask for recommendations, then combine the answers

Many of you are familiar with the two AI Search Visibility reports I released in [May](https://oppalerts.com/LLM-Ranking-Factors/)[1](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-1) and [July](https://oppalerts.com/AI-Search-Visibility/)[2](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-2) of this year.

I used the same 100 industries from the July report.

For each industry, I asked for the top 25 recommendations, 25 times, in 25 slightly different ways. For example:

*   “What are the 25 best hotels and resorts in the United States?”
*   “List the top 25 hotel and resort brands in the United States.”

That's 2,500 prompts. None names a brand, a persona, a city, or a price. Each asks for website domains, one per line, with the most recommended first.

I sent those prompts to 13 OpenAI models, from gpt-4o-mini through gpt-6-sol; three Google models, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gemini-3.8-flash; and ChatGPT through the web interface.

That's 16 LLMs through their APIs, plus ChatGPT web: 17 AI channels. The API tests used the models without web search. ChatGPT's web interface can search before answering.

I also ran the questions through Google and kept three separate lists: the organic results, the domains cited by AI Overviews, and the brands named by AI Overviews.

Those last two are different things. An AI Overview can recommend a hotel while citing a publisher that wrote about it.[3](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-3) I wanted to look at both.

One answer isn't enough to get a useful ranking. Ask again and the list can change.[4](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-4) So I combined all 25 answers for each industry and model, scoring each domain by how often it appeared and how high it appeared:

*   Position 1 gets 1 point.
*   Position 2 gets 1/2 point.
*   Position 3 gets 1/3 point, and so on.

Add those up across the 25 answers and you have the domain's AI score.[5](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-5) Sort by that score and you have its AI rank. A domain named first every time scores 25. A domain named once, in position 20, scores 0.05.

This is also why a list can have more than 25 brands. The answers don't all recommend the same ones. One gpt-4.1-nano list reached 571 domains.

Across all the answers, I collected 117,453 different domains. The analysis in this post uses up to the top 100 from each list: 55,862 domains, representing 70,003 combinations of domain and industry.

Some models give much shorter lists. GPT-6 Astra's median is 51 brands, and only eight of its industry lists reach 100. GPT-4o Mini fills 100 places in almost every industry. Keep that in mind when we get to the bottom of the charts.

## Find the pages linking to and mentioning those brands

OppAlerts has two search engines it maintains.

One is for news, including news sites, blogs, and podcasts.[6](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-6) It lets users monitor brands, competitors, and content relevant to their industry.

The other is for link and marketing opportunities: guest posts, product reviews, events, sponsorships, resource pages, etc.

Every page in both indexes already has an embedding of its main content. Each one is a list of 768 numbers.

So I had the recommendations, and I had the content and embeddings needed to look at their backlinks.

I searched the indexes for three sets of pages:

1.   **Backlinks:** pages that link to the domain. The analysis includes 28.4 million pairs of pages and brands: 9.7 million from the news index and 18.7 million from the prospect index.
2.   **Brand mentions:** pages that name the brand, whether or not they also link to it. This includes 56.2 million pairs of pages and brands.
3.   **Unlinked mentions:** pages that name the brand without linking to it. This includes 50.1 million pairs of pages and brands.

These are pairs because one page can link to or mention several brands. A page linking to Marriott and Hilton counts once for each.

Getting the brand names was its own piece of work. I drafted a name for each domain, checked it against the homepage title, and ran mention searches for 44,600 brand names. Brands that weren't searched are excluded from the mention analysis.

For 242 of the largest combinations of brand and index, the backlink search returned more than 50,000 pages. I scored the first 50,000 and kept the full count for the page totals. Across all brands, the full searches returned 136.5 million backlink matches.

Unless I say otherwise, the charts combine the news and prospect indexes. I also checked them separately, which I'll come back to.

## Figure out what those pages are about

Thankfully, other people have already spent a lot of time figuring out useful sets of business and content categories.

Those sets are called taxonomies.

I used four of them, from three different organizations, so that the research wouldn't depend on one organization's way of categorizing the world.

| Taxonomy[7](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-7) | Categories | Published by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google Ads Topics | 2,558 | Google |
| IAB Content | 704 | IAB Tech Lab |
| IAB Ad Product | 583 | IAB Tech Lab |
| NAICS | 2,125 | US Census Bureau |
| All four | 5,970 |  |

For every page, I compared its embedding with the embedding of every category.[8](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-8) That gives me 5,970 similarity scores per page.

Most of the charts below use Google Ads Topics, the largest taxonomy.

For the hotel industry, its closest category is “Hotels & Accommodations.” I put that on the left, then sort the other 2,557 categories by how similar they are to it. “Hospitality Industry” is nearby, along with other travel categories. At the far right is the least similar category, “Laser Vision Correction.”

![Image 1: Hotels and resorts in 3D: Hotels & Accommodations on the far left, Laser Vision Correction on the far right](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/00-3d-hotels-raw-ends-dark.webp)![Image 2: Hotels and resorts in 3D: Hotels & Accommodations on the far left, Laser Vision Correction on the far right](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/00-3d-hotels-raw-ends-light.webp)

Now I can take Marriott's backlinks, average their scores for each category, and see what Marriott's backlink profile looks like.

Then I can do the same for the second recommendation, the third, and all the way down the list. And then repeat that for the other industries and models.

## Add PageRank and PageRank over time

I also have PageRank records for these domains going back nine years, from July 2017 through September 2026. Of the full set of 117,453 domains, 86,053 have PageRank records.

The PageRank used here is a domain-level score on a scale from 0 to 100.[9](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-9)

PRoT, or PageRank over time, adds up a domain's PageRank across all of those records. It represents how long and how well a site has been established. A site that held a PageRank of 40 for nine years will have a much higher PRoT than a site that only reached 40 last year.

PRoT doesn't necessarily mean trust. But it wouldn't be much of a stretch to think of it as something like a trust factor.

That gives us a way to look at how established a site is, along with its current PageRank.

## What the backlink content shows

![Image 3: Backlinks to recommended brands and the relevance to their industry](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/01-core-curve-all-sources-dark.webp)![Image 4: Backlinks to recommended brands and the relevance to their industry](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/01-core-curve-all-sources-light.webp)

This chart combines all 100 industries for GPT-6 Astra.

Across the bottom are the 2,558 Google Ads Topics categories, ordered from most similar to the industry on the left to least similar on the right. The height shows the average similarity of the pages to each category.

The blue line is backlinks. Green is all brand mentions. Orange is mentions without links.

Each industry's categories are sorted in that industry's own order before I average them together. Every category has its own point in the chart.

You can see the same thing in all three lines. The pages are most similar to the categories closest to the industry's own category, and less similar as we move away from it.

The pages linking to hotel brands are, on balance, about hotels and related subjects. The same is true for the pages mentioning those brands, even when there's no link.

Here's that data in 3D, first for backlinks, then for unlinked mentions:

![Image 5: GPT-6 Astra across all industries: raw similarity of pages linking to recommended brands](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/02-3d-all-raw-chart-dark.webp)![Image 6: GPT-6 Astra across all industries: raw similarity of pages linking to recommended brands](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/02-3d-all-raw-chart-light.webp)

![Image 7: GPT-6 Astra across all industries: raw similarity of pages mentioning recommended brands without links](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/03-3d-all-unlinked-raw-chart-dark.webp)![Image 8: GPT-6 Astra across all industries: raw similarity of pages mentioning recommended brands without links](https://oppalerts.com/img/blog/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data/03-3d-all-unlinked-raw-chart-light.webp)

Each row is a brand, with AI rank 1 at the back. Each column is a category, with the industry's own category on the left. The height and color show the similarity score.

The charts show individual industries as well as averages across all 100.

As you move down the rankings toward rank 100, the backlink profiles get less focused. They still generally follow the same trend, but the curve gets choppier. Part of that is simply that lower-ranked brands have fewer backlinks. With only a handful of backlinks, a couple of unrelated pages can move the whole profile. The more backlinks a site has, the more they settle into a tighter pattern. So when you see the front rows of these charts looking noisier, that's what's going on. The section on why some of the charts get spiky goes into this in more detail.

## How often the pattern holds

I didn't want to rely on a chart that looked convincing. I counted how often the pattern held.

For the 17 AI channels plus the brands named in Google's AI Overviews, there are:

**18 channels × 100 industries × 4 taxonomies × 3 sets of pages = 21,600 curves.**

For each curve, I compared the average score of the most similar quarter of categories with the average of the least similar quarter.

All 21,600 passed.

I also ran a narrower test: compare just the industry's own category with the single least similar category. That passed in 21,593 cases.

The seven exceptions all came from one industry in one taxonomy: GPU and AI infrastructure vendors in IAB Ad Product. The industry's selected category is “Circuit Boards and Components,” while the least similar category is “Debated Sensitive Social Issue.” My guess is that pages about AI companies also discuss the public debate around AI. The broader quarter test still passes there.

Google's organic results and AI Overview citations were a little different, with 13 exceptions out of 2,400 curves. Those lists often point to publishers. For hotels, the top organic results include usnews.com, tripadvisor.com, revenuebase.ai, tophotelbrands.com, and cntraveler.com. A publisher's backlinks can cover a much wider set of topics.

So we have a very consistent relevance pattern across the recommended brands.

The next step is to look at what separates the first recommendation from the tenth, or the fiftieth.

These are medians across the industries represented at each rank. At rank 50, that's 57 industries. At rank 100, it's only eight. Page counts are rounded, and the half points in PageRank come from taking the median of an even number of brands.

For this test, a page counts as relevant when its similarity to the industry's category is at least two standard deviations above its average similarity across categories. In the charts and tables, that's a z-score of 2 or more.[10](https://oppalerts.com/we-now-know-the-1-ranking-factor-for-ai-and-llms-the-data#note-10)

In other words, the industry's category needs to stand out as something the page is strongly about.

The pattern in those medians is very strong. The correlation between AI rank and median link count is -0.96. Relevant links, unlinked mentions, PageRank, and PRoT are all between -0.95 and -0.97. The negative sign means the counts and scores get smaller as the rank number gets larger.
